methods.title: Estimate black-hole entropy from confined low-energy quanta
methods.principle: Combine gravitational radius, photon energy and total mass-energy
steps: Obtain the radius scale from G, mass and c
Limit a constituent massless wavelength to the object size
Infer the smallest constituent photon energy
Divide total mass-energy by that energy for the maximum-count scale
Multiply by k and compare with the supplied exact entropy formula
Evaluate the requested mass and interpret the large result
methods.boundary: The heuristic fixes scaling, not the exact numerical coefficient. The source uses h, not hbar, in its 8 pi squared coefficient.

methods.title: Balance gravitational binding against Fermi degeneracy energy
methods.principle: Equilibrium radius minimizes gravitational plus kinetic energy at fixed mass
steps: Choose the source density profile and gravitational binding coefficient
Convert total mass to the number of pressure-carrying fermions
Compute their filled-state kinetic energy as a function of radius
Minimize the total energy and check stability
Evaluate radius, density and validity scales
Repeat in the ultrarelativistic limit to identify a critical mass or loss of a stable minimum
methods.boundary: The uniform Newtonian model is an approximation. A zero coefficient of an inverse-radius energy is marginal, not a finite stable radius; neutron-star limits additionally require interactions and relativistic gravity.

methods.title: Calculate radiationless electron-ejection energies from shell binding energies
methods.principle: An inner vacancy releases energy that pays an outer electron binding energy and kinetic energy
steps: Identify the shell with the initial vacancy
Identify the electron filling it and the electron subsequently ejected
Express each energy relative to the same continuum zero
Subtract the filling-shell and ejected-shell binding energies from the vacancy-shell binding energy
Enumerate the channels requested and reject negative kinetic energies
State screening, ionization-shift and recoil approximations
methods.boundary: Adjacent shell gaps alone do not determine absolute Auger energies without at least one continuum-referenced binding energy. This is not merely photon emission from a two-level gap.

methods.title: Use or derive a semiclassical hydrogenic orbit
methods.principle: Coulomb centripetal balance plus quantized orbital angular momentum
steps: Set nuclear charge and the prescribed particle mass or reduced mass
Combine circular force balance with mvr=n hbar
Obtain radius, speed and kinetic and potential energies
Apply the energy reference at infinite separation
Calculate orbital period or ionization threshold as requested
Check that the one-electron semiclassical model is the intended approximation
methods.boundary: A Bohr orbit is not a literal modern stationary electron trajectory. Deriving the orbit equations is more work than substituting a quantum number into them.

methods.title: Construct and compare atomic electron configurations
methods.principle: Energy ordering plus Pauli exclusion and Hund filling determine ground occupation
steps: Determine electron count from nuclear charge and ionization
Fill the stated orbital energy order with correct subshell capacities
Resolve open-shell spin occupation using Hund first rule
Check known source exceptions rather than impose an exact universal filling mnemonic
Write the configuration and identify valence electrons
Compare group or period patterns while distinguishing shell index from filling order
methods.boundary: A configuration notation describes occupations, not automatically an exact many-body eigenstate or a full LS term. Main-group valence regularities need qualification for transition elements.

methods.title: Infer excitation gaps from electron energy-loss or Franck-Hertz data
methods.principle: Inelastic electron energy loss supplies target excitation energy
steps: Identify the elastic baseline or accelerating-voltage zero
Read loss-peak positions or repeated current-minimum spacing
Convert voltage intervals to energy for the projectile charge
Distinguish repeated excitations from different target levels
Construct the requested level diagram relative to its stated ground level
Convert an identified excitation gap into a photon wavelength if requested
methods.boundary: Contact and retarding potentials can shift absolute current-minimum voltages. In a multiple-collision tube the second dip is not automatically the second excited state. A loss spectrum may include collective excitations, not only single-atom levels.

methods.title: Compare atomic models against scattering and spectra
methods.principle: A physical model must account for measured charge concentration and discrete lines
steps: Identify the charge and mass distribution posited by each model
Predict qualitative scattering or stability consequences
Contrast them with the cited experimental observation
Identify which added assumptions explain discrete spectra
State remaining model limitations
methods.boundary: This is a conceptual model test, not a calculation of a particular bound-state energy.

methods.title: Estimate characteristic X-rays with a screened hydrogenic spectrum
methods.principle: Inner-shell energy gaps scale approximately with effective nuclear charge squared
steps: Identify the target atomic number and line or capture endpoint
Choose the source screening convention and shell indices
Evaluate the difference of screened hydrogenic binding energies
Convert to photon frequency or wavelength
Form same-line ratios between elements if requested
Distinguish this approximation from accurate many-electron atomic energies
methods.boundary: The source uses Z minus one screening for K-series estimates. Frequency scales with (Z-1) squared, not exactly Z squared. Characteristic lines are different from the bremsstrahlung cutoff.

methods.title: Explain orbital-energy splitting through penetration and screening
methods.principle: Different radial distributions sample different effective nuclear attraction
steps: Identify the orbitals and occupied inner shells being compared
Compare their probability of penetrating the screening electron cloud
Relate greater penetration to stronger nuclear attraction and increased binding
Explain why equal principal quantum number alone no longer fixes energy in a many-electron atom
methods.boundary: This is a qualitative screening argument,not construction of a full electron configuration or derivation of a radial quantum-defect spectrum.

methods.title: Convert reversible reaction work into cell voltage
methods.principle: Electrical work per reaction equals charge transferred times potential difference
steps: Combine half reactions and identify electron transfer count
Obtain the full-reaction Gibbs change
Divide available work per mole by transferred molar charge
Reverse the sign or interpretation for electrolysis
Distinguish reversible voltage from real losses
methods.boundary: Do not count electrons from the balanced overall reaction alone; they cancel from it.

methods.title: Write a reaction equilibrium constraint
methods.principle: The stoichiometric sum of chemical potentials vanishes
steps: Balance the reaction
Assign signed stoichiometric coefficients
Express an infinitesimal reaction extent
Set the Gibbs derivative with respect to extent to zero
Write the resulting relation among species chemical potentials
methods.boundary: This task does not yet solve equilibrium concentrations or assume particular activity formulas.

methods.title: Calculate equilibrium composition from reaction free energy and conservation
methods.principle: Dimensionless activities obey K=exp(-delta G standard/RT)
steps: Choose the correct gas, solute, pure-liquid and pure-solid standard states
Calculate the reaction standard Gibbs energy or use the supplied K
Build the activity product with stoichiometric powers
Impose atom conservation, charge neutrality and specified total pressure or volume
Solve for physical concentrations or reaction extent
Test approximations and distinguish equilibrium from reaction kinetics
methods.boundary: Partial pressures are divided by standard pressure and molalities by standard molality. Pure solvent and solid activities are approximately one only under their stated conditions.

methods.title: Derive a chemical equilibrium constant from molecular partition functions
methods.principle: Chemical potentials combine translational, internal and binding energies
steps: Choose a consistent energy reference including dissociation or ionization cost
Construct each species translational and internal partition factor
Include degeneracies and molecular symmetry without double counting
Insert chemical potentials into the balanced reaction constraint
Rearrange into the dimensionless standard-pressure equilibrium constant
Evaluate over temperature and solve illustrative composition balances
methods.boundary: Electronic and nuclear spin factors must be tracked separately. An arbitrary species energy shift changes reaction energetics unless binding offsets are transformed consistently.

methods.title: Convert between atomic composition, molar mass and particle count
methods.principle: Avogadro counting connects mass per particle and per mole
steps: Read the chemical formula and constituent masses
Sum atomic masses with their actual multiplicities
For ideal mixtures average using particle-number fractions, converting any mass fractions first
Convert molar mass to mass per particle using Avogadro number
Use total mass divided by molar mass for moles and multiply by Avogadro number for particle count
Distinguish atoms from molecules and multiply by atoms per molecule when needed
methods.boundary: A mole of H atoms is not a mole of H2 molecules; counts must name the elementary entity.

methods.title: Solve composition-dependent phase equilibrium from equal chemical potentials
methods.principle: Each exchangeable species has equal chemical potential across phases
steps: Differentiate the mixture free energy when the chemical potentials are not supplied
Include ideal mixing logarithms or the specified activity model
Equate chemical potentials of the same species across phases
Insert reference phase-change free energies and their temperature dependence
Solve for both coexistence compositions
Plot or fit the parameters requested
methods.boundary: The two species require two equilibrium conditions. A pure-substance crossing does not replace them.

methods.title: Compute reaction thermodynamic changes from formation data
methods.principle: Stoichiometric products-minus-reactants balance
steps: Balance the reaction and identify the phases and reference states
Multiply each tabulated formation quantity by its stoichiometric coefficient
Subtract reactant totals from product totals
When entropy is supplied use or check deltaG=deltaH-T*deltaS
Scale the per-mole change to the requested amount and apply the stated heat/work convention
methods.boundary: Formation entropies and absolute species entropies are not interchangeable. Finding equilibrium composition adds mass action and conservation.

methods.title: Derive or apply equilibrium-constant changes with temperature or pressure
methods.principle: log K equals minus the standard reaction Gibbs energy divided by RT
steps: Differentiate log K=-delta G standard/(R*T) with the other natural variable held fixed
Use the appropriate reaction Gibbs derivative: minus reaction entropy for temperature or reaction volume for pressure
For temperature combine delta G+T delta S=delta H;for pressure retain delta V
Integrate or linearize over the specified change,holding reaction enthalpy or volume constant only when justified
Evaluate the relative equilibrium constant and the validity of the extrapolation
methods.boundary: Temperature and pressure derivatives use different conjugate inputs and signs. This reaction-equilibrium calculation is not the osmotic-pressure relation also called van t Hoff.

methods.title: Solve a sinusoidal AC circuit with signed phasors
methods.principle: Complex voltage-current relations and Kirchhoff balances
steps: Choose a common sinusoidal phase reference and consistently use peak or rms values
Represent resistors, inductors and capacitors by R, i omega L and 1/(i omega C)
Combine impedances in series or admittances in parallel, or form node and loop equations
Solve for the requested complex currents and voltages
Recover magnitudes, quadrant-correct phases and instantaneous signals
Apply resonance by cancellation of reactive parts and retain both admissible frequency branches
Check the low- and high-frequency limits and sum instantaneous voltages rather than their magnitudes
methods.boundary: One-element, series and parallel problems use the same signed component procedure; a requested derivation or plotted phasor construction remains recorded. A full switching transient requires the homogeneous initial-value solution, not only steady phasors. A current resonance need not coincide with a capacitor-voltage resonance.

methods.title: Relate capacitor voltage buildup to delivered charge and current
methods.principle: Charge conservation and Q=CV
steps: Identify the capacitance and initial charge
Convert the target voltage into the required charge change
Relate current to charge per time
Integrate the stated constant or voltage-dependent current law
Stop at the physical cutoff condition
Check whether the assumed current law is supplied or only an idealization
methods.boundary: A stopping-voltage condition alone fixes final charge, not charging time without a current law.

methods.title: Find capacitor charge, voltage, field and stored energy at a specified constraint
methods.principle: Q=CV and U=Q squared over 2C with the applicable capacitance relation
steps: Identify geometry, dielectric and whether charge or voltage is held fixed
Evaluate the known capacitance formula or use a supplied capacitance
Solve Q=CV and the corresponding gap-field relation
Evaluate U=Q squared over 2C or CV squared over 2 when requested
For a change, apply the electrical constraint before comparing states
Check the field limit, signs and geometry approximation
methods.boundary: This is application of established capacitance and energy formulas. Explicit derivation by Gauss law, integration of field energy, network reduction and mechanical work need their own requested steps. A fixed-voltage source exchanges energy when C changes.

methods.title: Relate ideal-transformer turns, voltages, currents and reflected load
methods.principle: Common linked flux per turn and lossless power transfer
steps: Identify primary and secondary turns and whether voltages are peak or rms
Use V2/V1=N2/N1 for the same waveform
Use equal input and output power to infer the inverse current ratio
Reflect a secondary load to the primary by (N1/N2) squared when requested
Include rectifier and peak-holding assumptions only when the source supplies them
Check that steady DC cannot sustain the alternating-flux relation
methods.boundary: Not a real-transformer safety or rating calculation. Winding resistance, leakage, core loss, magnetizing current and saturation are excluded unless stated.

methods.title: Relate inductor flux linkage, voltage, current and stored energy
methods.principle: Linear flux linkage and signed induced emf
steps: Identify self or mutual inductance and the relevant source and recipient windings
Use linked flux=L I or M I; divide by recipient turns only for per-turn flux
Differentiate current and use emf=-L di/dt or -M di/dt with a consistent terminal convention
Use U=L I squared/2 for self-field energy when requested
Infer unknown quantities and distinguish current from its rate of change
methods.boundary: Applies a known inductance or known geometry formula. Deriving inductance by a field calculation or flux integral is a separate task. Magnetic materials must be in the stated linear regime; mutual energy depends on relative winding sense.

methods.title: Find an infinite ladder resistance from its self-similar tail
methods.principle: The remaining infinite network has the same terminal resistance as the whole
steps: Separate the first cell from the remaining network
Replace the tail by the unknown total resistance
Reduce the first cell to obtain a fixed-point equation
Solve and retain the nonnegative physically admissible root
Use voltage division to recover the attenuation per cell when requested
methods.boundary: An ordinary finite network reduction does not establish the self-consistent tail resistance. Use positive resistances and the passive limit of finite networks.

methods.title: Reduce a series-parallel component network and recover individual drops and flows
methods.principle: Node connectivity, common parallel potential differences and conserved series flow or charge
steps: Mark nodes joined by ideal wires
Identify genuine parallel pairs and series pairs with an unbranched intermediate node
Use the component-specific combination rule to replace a subnetwork
Repeat to find the terminal equivalent
Undo reductions to recover every requested branch voltage and charge or current
Check node conservation and terminal sums
methods.boundary: For capacitors, parallel capacitances add and reciprocal capacitances add in series; equal series charges require initially neutral isolated intermediate nodes. For resistors, series resistances add and reciprocal resistances add in parallel. A bridge not reducible this way needs node or loop equations. Uncoupled inductors add in series and reciprocally in parallel. Mutual coupling requires its signed cross terms and cannot be silently ignored.

methods.title: Reduce a network by symmetry-equivalent node potentials
methods.principle: Uniqueness of the node-equation solution under a symmetry that preserves the terminals
steps: Identify permutations preserving the entire network and imposed terminal potentials
Conclude that nodes exchanged by these permutations have equal potentials
Merge these nodes without introducing current between unequal potentials
Reduce the resulting series-parallel network
Recover equivalent resistance and requested branch currents
methods.boundary: Visual similarity alone is insufficient: the chosen source terminals must preserve the symmetry. This is an additional argument beyond ordinary series-parallel reduction.

methods.title: Infer particle charge-to-mass ratio from beam measurements
methods.principle: Eliminate beam speed and particle count between deflection, charge and energy measurements
steps: State the electric and magnetic field regions and measured screen geometry
Relate magnetic curvature or angular deflection to charge-to-mass ratio and speed
Relate speed either to crossed-field cancellation or to collected heat and charge
Eliminate unmeasured speed and particle number
Infer charge-to-mass ratio or an unknown field parameter
Check the small-angle and nonrelativistic assumptions and parameter identifiability
methods.boundary: A charge-to-mass measurement alone cannot determine charge and mass separately. An unknown stray field requires its spatial extent and direction, not merely a changed fitted ratio.

methods.title: Relate field or potential jumps to a surface charge
methods.principle: Normal electric-field jump and tangential continuity
steps: Choose a common unit normal
Evaluate both one-sided fields or potential derivatives
Subtract with the same orientation
Compare normal jump with surface charge over permittivity
Check tangential field and potential continuity
methods.boundary: These electrostatic conditions concern an ordinary surface charge, not an ideal dipole sheet with a potential jump.

methods.title: Replace a specified polarization by its bound charge distribution
methods.principle: Volume minus divergence and surface normal polarization
steps: Identify every material region and its outward normal
Compute minus divergence of the polarization within each region
Compute the normal polarization on all outer and inner surfaces
At an interface combine the two one-sided surface contributions
Include distributional point or sheet terms where the polarization is singular
Integrate to check total bound charge
methods.boundary: Uniform polarization is a constant vector, not a radial vector of constant magnitude. A cavity inner normal points into the cavity.

methods.title: Derive capacitance from charge and potential difference
methods.principle: C equals Q divided by conductor potential difference
steps: Assign equal opposite trial charges
Determine the field in the gap
Integrate between conductor surfaces
Divide the charge by the resulting potential difference
Use per-length quantities for infinite conductors
Check dimensions and limiting geometry

methods.title: Relate capacitor displacement work to field energy
methods.principle: Energy conservation at the stated electrical constraint
steps: Identify whether charge is fixed or a voltage source remains connected
Determine the force or field-energy density
Express the displaced volume and mechanical work
Calculate the corresponding field-energy change
Include source work if charge is transferred
Compare signs
methods.boundary: Fixed-charge and fixed-voltage experiments cannot use the same energy balance without the voltage-source contribution.

methods.title: Determine visibility from a source worldline
methods.principle: Intersections of past light rays with a timelike trajectory
steps: Sketch the source worldline and its limiting asymptotes
Draw both outgoing null directions from representative events
Solve or bound the light-cone intersection condition
Identify the observable and unobservable spacetime regions
Determine the first-arrival time or limiting horizon
Test whether a continuously timelike source can later leave the observer past light cone
methods.boundary: A horizon boundary reached only from infinite past source time is not an ordinary finite-time emission event.

methods.title: Count elementary charges and track a net charge
methods.principle: Charge is conserved and net charge is the signed sum over carriers
steps: Identify the species and charge per carrier
Find particle counts from mass, number density or the supplied transfer
Sum signed carrier charges or divide a charge imbalance by elementary charge
Track equal and opposite changes when charge transfers between isolated bodies
Distinguish total electron charge from net object charge
methods.boundary: Atomic particle counting may require a separate molar-mass step. Effective molecular partial charges need not be integer elementary charges; isolated free-particle charges do.

methods.title: Relate charge accumulation to the divergence or boundary flux of current
methods.principle: Local and integral charge conservation
steps: Identify the charge-storing region and the oriented current through its boundary
Write dQ/dt=-outward integral J dot da,or partial rho/partial t=-div J
Use the specified symmetry to relate a local current to the total boundary flux
Integrate in space or time with the given initial or boundary value
In a steady state set accumulation to zero,not the individual through-currents
methods.boundary: Current density rho times carrier velocity is a distinct constitutive description. A region may carry a nonzero steady through-current without acquiring net charge.

methods.title: Explain contact charging, induction and discharge
methods.principle: Mobile charge redistributes subject to charge conservation and electrical connection constraints
steps: Specify initially charged, neutral, conducting and insulating objects
Follow which carriers can move and whether grounding or contact is present
Track redistribution before contact and net transfer during contact
Remove connections in the stated order and conserve charge on each newly isolated system
Use the final signs and induced distributions to explain attraction, repulsion or discharge
methods.boundary: Attraction does not alone prove opposite net signs: charged-neutral and some close unequal like-charged conductors can attract. Do not assign a triboelectric sign without material/contact information.

methods.title: Calculate electrical power, transferred energy and the complete circuit energy budget
methods.principle: Signed power equals voltage times current; resistive heat is nonnegative
steps: Identify the voltage and current through the component and their relative sign
Use P=VI and, for a resistor, I squared R or V squared over R
Integrate power over the requested time when energy is wanted
Separate internal source losses from useful terminal output and chemical conversion
Include stored electric or magnetic energy changes and maintained-source work when relevant
Check the total energy balance if requested
methods.boundary: Emf times current is chemical conversion, not necessarily terminal output. Energy delivered at approximately constant battery voltage is VQ, while charging an initially empty ideal capacitor stores QV/2. A quoted equivalent lighting wattage is not the actual electrical power.

methods.title: Form circuit equations with signed voltage drops and charge continuity
methods.principle: Kirchhoff node and loop balances with the stated element laws
steps: Mark circuit nodes, loop directions and source polarities
Apply charge-current continuity at every relevant junction
Write each resistor, capacitor, source and induced-emf relation with consistent signs
Write independent loop or node equations
Solve the algebraic equations for steady states, or reduce to the required initial-value equations for time-dependent states
Recover requested branch currents and node-potential differences
Check open circuits, short circuits and ideal-meter assumptions
methods.boundary: A capacitor has zero steady DC current but may have nonzero voltage; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance and an ideal voltmeter infinite resistance. This setup does not replace solving a transient differential equation; retain initial capacitor charge and continuous inductor current.

methods.title: Find induced surface charges and fields in conductor cavities
methods.principle: Zero field in metal, equipotential boundaries and charge conservation
steps: Separate metal, cavities and exterior
Use a Gaussian surface within the metal to fix each cavity-wall total
Enforce conductor total charge or grounded potential
Use only the symmetry surviving in each region to find surface density and field
Exclude particle self fields when calculating force
State which regions are shielded from external changes
methods.boundary: An off-center charge need not experience zero force. External fields may change the outer-surface density without changing a closed cavity field.

methods.title: Redistribute charge between electrically connected conductors
methods.principle: Connected electrostatic conductors share a potential and conserve their combined isolated charge
steps: Write the potential of each conductor including mutual contributions unless a well-separated approximation is justified
Set connected conductor potentials equal
Conserve total charge or impose the specified grounded potential
Solve the charge allocation
Calculate surface fields from local geometry and charge
State neglected wire charge and mutual-polarization corrections
methods.boundary: Equal potentials do not imply equal charges or equal surface fields. The simple q/R rule assumes well-separated spheres; a finite separation requires mutual terms.

methods.title: Derive energy and momentum conservation from field equations
methods.principle: Eliminate sources from electrical work and Lorentz force densities
steps: Begin with the specified total or free source work and force laws
Substitute the matching Maxwell equations
Use product rules to separate time derivatives and spatial divergences
Identify energy and momentum densities and their fluxes
Integrate over a volume if required
Retain material or magnetic-charge terms consistently
methods.boundary: Vacuum, hypothetical magnetic charges and macroscopic free-source bookkeeping share this derivation strategy but do not justify silently interchanging their source laws or material momentum conventions.

methods.title: Convert moving charge to current and normalize its distribution
methods.principle: Current density equals signed mobile charge density times velocity
steps: Identify which charge species move
Write their velocity including rotational position dependence
Multiply charge density by velocity with the correct line, surface or volume measure
Sum species if needed
Integrate through the cross section to fix a specified total current
Distinguish carrier drift speed from signal speed
methods.boundary: Stationary compensating charge contributes to electric density but not current.

methods.title: Match electric and displacement fields at a dielectric interface
methods.principle: Tangential electric continuity and normal displacement jump
steps: Resolve fields normal and parallel to the interface
Enforce continuous tangential electric field
Set the normal displacement jump to free surface charge
Substitute each medium constitutive law
Solve for field components or refraction angles
Recover bound charge separately from polarization
methods.boundary: Zero free surface charge does not imply continuous normal electric field when permittivities differ.

methods.title: Compute assembly energy including linear polarization response
methods.principle: One half the volume integral of electric field dot displacement
steps: Specify what is assembled and whether the dielectric responds
Determine E and D in each region
Integrate one half E dot D for a lossless linear material
Include vacuum regions
Compare with epsilon-zero E-squared over two if purely macroscopic electrostatic energy is also requested
Do not use the linear-response expression for frozen polarization or hysteresis
methods.boundary: For general reversible nonlinear media integrate E dot dD along the constitutive path; the factor one half is not universal.

methods.title: Explain dielectric screening, polarization and its material limits
methods.principle: Bound-charge response opposes the imposed field while free conduction permits leakage
steps: Distinguish bound displacement or dipole alignment from freely transported charge
Relate polarization direction to the induced surface signs
Distinguish externally fixed free charge from a maintained voltage
Explain the relevant thermal disorder, leakage or breakdown mechanism
Separate the dimensionless response coefficient from a field-strength failure threshold
methods.boundary: A large dielectric constant does not imply high breakdown strength or low leakage. A perfect conductor is a formal zero-static-interior-field limit, not an ordinary lossless dielectric at arbitrary frequency.

methods.title: Solve self-consistent electric or magnetic material response
methods.principle: Applied field plus a known shape-dependent response field and the specified constitutive law
steps: Distinguish the applied,total macroscopic and microscopic or auxiliary fields
Write the known geometry-dependent depolarizing or demagnetizing field
Use E=Eapplied+Epolarization or H=B/mu0-M with the appropriate shape relation
Insert the stated electric polarizability,susceptibility or magnetic response law
Solve the resulting algebraic feedback relation for polarization or magnetization
Recover all requested fields and check the stated material and phase limits
methods.boundary: Electric susceptibility normally multiplies the macroscopic E;magnetic susceptibility multiplies H,not B/mu0. Atomic polarizability uses the local field excluding that atom. Meissner B=0 is an imposed equilibrium-phase constraint,not a consequence of arbitrary perfect-conductor history.

methods.title: Relate dipole orientation, moment and interaction energy
methods.principle: Negative dipole-field dot product
steps: When the energy formula itself must be derived,integrate minus the dipole torque over orientation with an explicit energy reference
Write the interaction energy as minus the dipole-field scalar product
Insert the two orientations or infer the moment from the field coefficient
Compare energies to identify the lower-energy alignment
Form an energy difference if a radiative transition is requested

methods.title: Find displacement current and its magnetic effect
methods.principle: Time derivative of electric displacement and Ampere-Maxwell circulation
steps: Obtain the electric field and the appropriate material displacement
Differentiate in time
Integrate its normal component through the specified surface
Add conduction current through that same surface
Apply symmetry to obtain B when justified
Compare magnitudes and phases when testing a quasistatic approximation
methods.boundary: Use epsilon-zero E in vacuum and D in a material. Surface independence involves conduction plus displacement current, not either one separately.

methods.title: Transform electric and magnetic sources and fields together
methods.principle: Duality symmetry of Maxwell equations and the force law
steps: Fix the magnetic-charge convention and SI factors
Apply the same electric-magnetic rotation to fields and source densities
Substitute into every equation
Group sine and cosine terms into the original equations
Transform the force law and show its invariance
Recover the pure electric-to-magnetic special case
methods.boundary: A field substitution without transforming charges and currents is not the full symmetry; magnetic charge here is hypothetical.

methods.title: Organize source, potential and field equations with their constraints
methods.principle: Equivalent differential and causal integral formulations
steps: Identify source densities and their continuity constraint
Identify potentials and the imposed gauge
Write the potential-source differential and retarded-integral links
Write field-potential derivative relations
Write Maxwell source-field equations and the causal field integrals
Exclude inverse links that the problem explicitly does not request
methods.boundary: A diagram of relationships is the requested output; substituting one numerical field calculation does not fulfill it.

methods.title: Integrate linear or angular momentum stored in fields
methods.principle: Momentum density epsilon-zero E cross B
steps: Find the overlapping electric and magnetic fields throughout space
Form the full vector cross product before using symmetry
Integrate momentum density with the proper volume element
For angular momentum take position cross momentum density about the specified origin first
Include all interior and exterior regions and any contact contribution
Check convergence, direction and conservation comparisons
methods.boundary: Angular momentum is not generally the moment arm of a point charge crossed with the total field momentum. Static fields can carry both quantities.

methods.title: Distinguish ideal-conductor flux freezing from Meissner expulsion
methods.principle: Ohm law and Faraday induction
steps: Take the infinite-conductivity zero-electric-field limit
Use Faraday law to show the internal magnetic field cannot change in that ideal-conductor limit
Retain the initial field history
Contrast with the separate equilibrium Meissner property

methods.title: Prove conservation or evolution of flux through a moving loop
methods.principle: Moving-surface transport and Faraday law
steps: Relate the two loop positions by an infinitesimal swept ribbon
Use divergence B=0 to replace the surface difference by ribbon flux
Express ribbon flux as a velocity cross field line integral
Apply Stokes theorem and the local induction equation
Combine explicit field change with material motion
Apply the stated conductivity assumption
methods.boundary: Perfect conductivity freezes existing flux but does not by itself expel it; Meissner exclusion is an additional property.

methods.title: Check or impose a gauge without changing physical fields
methods.principle: A shifts by grad lambda while V shifts by minus d lambda/dt
steps: Evaluate the original divergence and scalar time derivative
Check Coulomb and Lorenz conditions independently
Apply or solve for the supplied gauge function
Derive its Poisson or wave equation for the requested gauge
Verify that the transformed E and B are unchanged
State topology, boundary and residual-gauge restrictions
methods.boundary: A=0 is impossible for nonzero B. V=0 can be chosen by a temporal gauge transformation locally, but that need not preserve another requested gauge or asymptotic convention.

methods.title: Solve plane-interface or wedge problems with reflected images
methods.principle: Boundary matching and uniqueness in the physical region
steps: Reflect source positions across each plane
Determine image signs, orientations and amplitudes by the actual boundary conditions
Iterate reflections for multiple planes when necessary
Verify all interface conditions and the allowed physical region
Add real and image potentials or fields
Exclude each real source own field for force and use induced-response energy for work
methods.boundary: Grounded conductors, dielectric transmission/reflection and magnetic flux exclusion share the reflection construction but have different boundary equations. Images are not independent physical sources for assembly energy.

methods.title: Solve spherical or cylindrical conductor boundaries with inversion images
methods.principle: Inversion geometry gives the constant source-distance ratio on a circular or spherical boundary
steps: Choose the physical domain and the three-dimensional point-source or two-dimensional line-source potential kernel
Locate inverse image positions,or fit the inverse image pair for the two-conductor geometry
Choose image strengths so each conductor boundary is equipotential
Add center or reference contributions to impose specified potentials,total charges or neutrality
Differentiate the verified physical-region potential for fields,surface density and force
Use the responding-conductor energy convention for work and check grounding,reference and large-distance limits
methods.boundary: Spherical point-source and cylindrical logarithmic kernels have different image strengths;do not copy the sphere charge factor into the line problem. Images lie outside the physical solution domain and are not independent physical charges for assembly work.

methods.title: Test force claims when conducting charges redistribute
methods.principle: Self-consistent induced charge response and electrostatic energy
steps: Separate imposed charge from induced charge
Determine what changes when the external source moves or reverses
Use symmetry or a concrete admissible geometry to test the claim
Relate force to the derivative of the minimized energy when useful
Distinguish a uniform external field from field gradients
methods.boundary: Do not assume induced charges stay fixed or that every neutral conducting shape attracts in every geometry.

methods.title: Calculate self or mutual inductance from linked magnetic flux
methods.principle: Flux linkage per source current and reciprocal mutual coupling
steps: Select which circuit carries a trial current
Calculate its field in the other loop or in every turn
Integrate and sum the linked flux
Divide by the source current
Use mutual reciprocity to choose an easier source circuit when permitted
Retain finite wire radius or distributed-current weighting where necessary
methods.boundary: Self-inductance of an ideal zero-radius wire diverges. For distributed current an energy calculation may be simpler than flux linkage. A required direct calculation in both directions cannot be replaced by asserting reciprocity.

methods.title: Find an induced electric field using symmetry and circulation
methods.principle: Faraday circulation with magnetic flux derivative
steps: Determine the symmetry-allowed field direction
Choose a contour on which the tangential field integral simplifies
Integrate the changing magnetic flux through it
Solve for E in each region
Fix additive curl-free terms using actual boundary conditions
Check quasistatic limits and interface behavior
methods.boundary: Faraday law alone fixes a curl, not a unique field; infinite uniform changing B without boundary information is underdetermined.

methods.title: Find induced emf, current or transferred charge from flux change
methods.principle: Faraday law for a specified physical loop
steps: Choose the oriented loop and its spanning surface
Obtain B and integrate its normal component including turns
Differentiate the total flux using both motion and explicit time dependence as needed
Apply Lenz law to fix current direction
Use the circuit resistance or retain inductive dynamics when not negligible
Integrate current for total transferred charge when requested
methods.boundary: Blind differentiation across a switch changing the material loop, or an extended conductor with sliding contacts, can fail; use the force-per-charge path integral there.

methods.title: Evaluate a motional emf or meter reading along its actual path
methods.principle: Line integral of electric plus motional force per charge
steps: Specify the physical conductor or meter path and its velocity
Find E and the local velocity cross B as appropriate
Integrate the tangential force per charge along the path
Include the enclosed changing flux when relating different paths
Use resistive drops or conductor equilibrium to determine terminal measurements
Check signs against the stated terminal convention
methods.boundary: In a changing magnetic field a voltmeter reading can depend on its leads and path; it is not a unique scalar potential difference between two points.

methods.title: Estimate classical radiation from an accelerated point charge
methods.principle: Nonrelativistic Larmor power proportional to charge squared and acceleration squared
steps: Infer the acceleration from the specified trajectory or force
Evaluate q squared a squared divided by 6 pi epsilon-zero c cubed
Compare radiated energy per unit time with the particle energy
Check nonrelativistic applicability and distinguish this classical model from stationary quantum states
methods.boundary: Using the given power law is not a derivation from retarded radiation fields. A steady continuous current has different coherent-source cancellation.

methods.title: Recover sources and verify an electromagnetic field pair
methods.principle: All four Maxwell equations plus charge continuity
steps: Calculate both divergences and both curls including time derivatives
Infer charge and current from the sourced equations
Retain distributional point, line, shell and interface terms
Check the two homogeneous equations and charge continuity
Verify integral laws across singular sources
Interpret the inferred source motion and boundary conditions
methods.boundary: Checking only away from a singular source or checking only one curl equation is not a complete verification.

methods.title: Calculate mutual inductance from two line integrals
methods.principle: Neumann double line integral
steps: Parametrize both oriented wire loops
Form the tangent-vector dot product and point separation
Integrate the reciprocal-separation kernel over both loops
Reduce by relative-angle symmetry
Expand in a stated small parameter only where justified
Check exchange symmetry and compare any independent flux result
methods.boundary: The arbitrary-radius expansion and small-recipient-loop limit must preserve their different approximation assumptions.

methods.title: Find resistance from a spatial current distribution
methods.principle: Steady continuity and local Ohm law
steps: Use steady continuity to identify conserved current through successive sections
Express current density in terms of total current and area
Divide by the local conductivity to obtain E
Integrate E between electrodes or solve the corresponding boundary problem
Form voltage divided by current
Include series or parallel spreading regions correctly
methods.boundary: A position-dependent conductivity need not give a charge-free resistive medium or the vacuum electrostatic field profile.

methods.title: Relate orbital magnetic moment to angular momentum
methods.principle: Current-loop dipole moment
steps: Find the orbital period and charge current
Multiply by the enclosed area to obtain the dipole moment
Write the mechanical angular momentum
Eliminate the orbit radius and speed and retain the charge sign

methods.title: Obtain the field of a relative nuclear orbit
methods.principle: Circular current and Biot-Savart field
steps: Use the relative orbital speed and radius to compute the nuclear current
Evaluate the magnetic field at the electron at the loop center
Eliminate speed in favor of orbital angular momentum
Compare sign and magnitude with the low-speed transformed electric field

methods.title: Calculate or balance electric and magnetic forces on a moving charge
methods.principle: The signed Lorentz force q(E+v cross B)
steps: Specify the charge sign,velocity and actual external fields
Resolve velocity cross magnetic field in a common basis
Add the electric contribution and any separately stated mechanical force
For steady transverse motion set the corresponding force component to zero;otherwise retain the requested nonzero force
Solve for the requested force,speed,field or carrier density and check directions
methods.boundary: A full trajectory requires integration of the equation of motion. Negative carrier velocity is opposite conventional current.

methods.title: Derive weak-field polarizability from a displaced charge-cloud model
methods.principle: Equilibrium between applied and internal restoring fields
steps: Integrate the cloud density to obtain its internal field
Expand near the cloud center to the first nonzero restoring term
Balance that field against the applied field
Relate displacement to dipole moment
Extract the coefficient or nonlinear power of the field
State the displacement and weak-field assumptions
methods.boundary: A finite nonzero central density gives the linear leading restoring field in a spherical model; a vanishing central density can give nonlinear response.

methods.title: Derive particle momentum and energy equations in potentials
methods.principle: Lorentz force with convective derivative and canonical momentum
steps: Substitute the scalar/vector potential expressions into the Lorentz force
Use vector product identities with velocity independent of spatial differentiation
Separate partial time change from velocity dot spatial gradient
Identify mechanical versus canonical momentum
Dot with velocity for the energy equation when requested
Check gauge dependence of intermediates and the unchanged physical force
methods.boundary: The derivative of A along a moving particle is not its fixed-position partial time derivative; the velocity-dependent generalized potential is not simply electrostatic potential energy.

methods.title: Recover electric and magnetic fields from scalar and vector potentials
methods.principle: E=-grad V-partial A/partial t and B=curl A with a consistent gauge
steps: Identify the potentials and gauge;for a quasistatic source use its established instantaneous potential only within that approximation
For a requested pure-induction derivation,use B=curl A and Faraday law,then fix the remaining gradient by the specified gauge and boundary conditions
Differentiate at fixed observation coordinates,including explicit time dependence and implicit moving-source or retarded-time dependence
Form both fields and retain one-sided or distributional terms at singular boundaries
Check the requested source equations and distinguish a partial time derivative from the total derivative along a moving particle
methods.boundary: E=-partial A/partial t alone is valid only when the scalar contribution is absent in the chosen setup. Knowing A at an isolated point does not fix its spatial curl. A quasistatic potential is not an exact retarded source solution.

methods.title: Find electromagnetic power flow and check energy balance
methods.principle: Poynting vector and local work-energy conservation
steps: Obtain E and B in the region and on its boundary
Form E cross B divided by mu-zero or the specified material energy flux
Integrate the oriented normal flux over the relevant surface
Compute stored field-energy change and charge work when requested
Check local divergence or total power balance
Distinguish inward from outward flux
For a traveling plane wave relate mean intensity to mean energy density times wave speed
Distinguish peak, rms and nonoscillating fields before taking a time average; do not insert a factor of one half for a constant-magnitude field
methods.boundary: A nonzero static Poynting vector is possible. Integrating only a convenient surface patch is insufficient unless all other contributions vanish.

methods.title: Infer resistance, temperature or current using a resistivity-temperature relation
methods.principle: The stated rho(T) law and fixed-geometry R proportional to rho
steps: Identify the law and its reference temperature
Use the specified temperature coefficient and retain its reference in ratios
Relate measured resistance to V/I or given geometry
Solve the temperature-resistance relation or compare its values at two temperatures
Apply the actual fixed-voltage or fixed-current constraint for power
Check validity of the linear approximation and any ignored thermal expansion
methods.boundary: A coefficient tabulated at one reference temperature cannot be reused as though defined at another without adjustment, unless the problem explicitly instructs that approximation. Metallic self-heating generally raises R; semiconductor response may have the opposite sign.

methods.title: Differentiate a retarded trajectory quantity
methods.principle: Implicit differentiation of the light-cone condition
steps: Differentiate the light-cone equation in the requested observation variable
Solve for the derivative of retarded time
Propagate it through source position, velocity and acceleration
Differentiate the retarded denominator with the product rule
Combine terms without mixing present and retarded quantities
Check the constant-velocity and static limits

methods.title: Find potentials from time-dependent continuous sources
methods.principle: Retarded Green-function source integral
steps: Specify the source position variables and observation point
Replace source time by t minus source-observer distance over c
Determine the actual retarded support of switched or moving sources
Integrate the scalar density or oriented current kernel
Retain delta-function Jacobians when present
Check the causal front and static or slow-change limits
methods.boundary: Integrating retarded density is not the same as total charge on a simultaneous spatial slice. Replacing time by retarded time in a static field formula misses derivative terms.

methods.title: Evaluate potentials or fields of a moving point charge
methods.principle: Retarded light-cone intersection and Lienard-Wiechert expressions
steps: Solve the trajectory light-cone equation and select the past root
Check whether a retarded intersection actually exists
Evaluate source position, velocity and acceleration at that same time
Form the retarded distance and one-minus-direction-dot-beta factor
Insert them into the required potentials or velocity/acceleration fields
Verify special limits and distinguish retarded from present separation
methods.boundary: A uniformly moving source permits special present-position simplifications; accelerating motion generally does not. A causal horizon can remove the retarded root in part of spacetime.

methods.title: Derive the space-charge-limited diode law
methods.principle: Poisson equation plus energy and steady current continuity
steps: Write the one-dimensional Poisson equation
Relate electron speed to potential by energy conservation
Express constant current density as charge density times velocity
Eliminate density and speed to obtain the nonlinear potential equation
Integrate with zero cathode field and the plate potentials
Recover current, density, velocity profiles and scaling
methods.boundary: Uses cold emission, steady planar flow, negligible edge effects and the source nonrelativistic model.

methods.title: Explain absence of classical radiation from a steady continuous charge distribution
methods.principle: Time-independent charge and current distribution
steps: Distinguish accelerating individual carriers from the full charge/current density
Take the continuous steady-distribution limit
Identify constant electromagnetic multipole moments
Explain cancellation of radiative fields
methods.boundary: This classical source argument does not establish immunity of real excited atomic states to spontaneous emission.

methods.title: Calculate force or momentum flux using Maxwell stress
methods.principle: Surface traction and field-momentum balance
steps: Choose a closed surface enclosing exactly the target charges or currents
Determine the total field on each surface piece
Construct the needed tensor components or tensor-normal contraction
Integrate oriented traction over all pieces
Subtract the time derivative of enclosed field momentum in a nonstatic case
Relate negative stress to outward momentum flux where requested
methods.boundary: Stress-force integration is a distinct required route when the textbook asks for it; a direct pairwise Coulomb or current-element calculation alone does not fulfill that request.

methods.title: Calculate the force on charged surfaces after removing the self field
methods.principle: Surface density times the average one-sided electric field
steps: Find the limiting fields on both sides
Average to remove the infinitesimal local patch self field
Multiply by surface charge density
Project onto the requested force direction
Integrate over the selected surface
Check whether the conductor specialization is applicable
methods.boundary: For a conductor the pressure is epsilon-zero E-out-squared over two, but the surface normal varies over a curved object.

methods.title: Relate electric and magnetic fields of uniformly translating sources
methods.principle: For a common constant source velocity, B=v cross E/c squared
steps: Identify the common laboratory source velocity
Obtain or use the electric field in that same frame
Evaluate the oriented cross product with velocity
Divide by c squared and check directions and limits
methods.boundary: This relates fields, not particle forces. It is not a general identity for accelerating sources or sources with different velocities.

methods.title: Transfer a known solution through an exact field-equation analogy
methods.principle: Matching equations, sources and boundary data
steps: List the governing equations for both problems
Map each field, source and coefficient consistently
Check that the same domain and boundary conditions survive the map
Substitute the known solution
Convert the auxiliary mapped field to the physical requested field
Verify limiting cases
methods.boundary: Matching one visual geometry or one formula is not enough; constitutive conventions and contact terms can change the final physical field.

methods.title: Build a continuous source incrementally and integrate its assembly work
methods.principle: Potential of already assembled source times added source
steps: Choose an assembly parameter and the source already present
Calculate the added charge or mass element
Find the potential produced by the existing source at the addition point
Form the incremental work without double counting
Integrate over the assembly parameter
Compare with the final self energy

methods.title: Evaluate a volume-averaged source field by reversing its kernel
methods.principle: Source-observer interchange and the known uniform-ball field
steps: Write the vector field average as a volume integral
Reverse source and observation roles with the correct sign
Identify the equivalent uniform-ball source
Evaluate its interior or exterior field using Gauss law
Restore normalization
Sum point-source contributions or integrate the original density
methods.boundary: An internal-source volume average is not the internal-source surface average.

methods.title: Integrate the force on a continuous source region
methods.principle: Density times the external field and internal action-reaction cancellation
steps: Identify the material region whose net force is wanted
Exclude its self field or justify cancellation of all internal pairs
Express the usable total or external field
Multiply by the local source density
Project and integrate over the region
State why a surface-pressure shortcut does or does not apply

methods.title: Explain why a source density alone does not fix a field
methods.principle: Homogeneous solutions and missing boundary data
steps: Compute the density associated with the proposed field
Identify another field with the same divergence and curl
Show their difference is source-free
Determine which boundary or infinite-source limiting procedure selects a direction
Avoid imposing unprovided symmetry on the field

methods.title: Represent concentrated charge or mass by delta distributions
methods.principle: Integrated density must recover the prescribed source
steps: Identify the support of each source
Insert deltas in the constrained coordinates
Include the coordinate Jacobian in normalization
Superpose signed sources
Integrate over all space to check the total

methods.title: Find force on a small electric or current-loop magnetic dipole
methods.principle: Gradient of moment dotted with the external field, with instantaneous moment held fixed
steps: Find the external field excluding the dipole own response
Express field and moment in a fixed basis and retain all spatial derivatives
Take the gradient of moment dot field while holding the moment fixed
Only afterward substitute any induced-moment relation
Integrate moment density for an extended dilute polarized body,or insert the force into a stated balance
Check the small-object approximation and the curl term before replacing the gradient by a directional derivative
methods.boundary: For electrostatics grad(p dot E)=(p dot grad)E. For a current-loop magnetic dipole grad(m dot B)=(m dot grad)B+m cross curl B; the last term cannot be dropped inside source currents. Differentiating an induced electric moment inside -p dot E incorrectly doubles its force.

methods.title: Find dipole torque and rotational equilibrium
methods.principle: Moment cross external field
steps: Find the external field at the dipole center
Compute moment cross field
Find zero-torque orientations
Test the restoring direction or orientation-energy curvature
Add position cross net force if changing the torque origin
methods.boundary: Torques about two different centers need not be equal and opposite. A grounded-image response depends on the dipole orientation.

methods.title: Compute energy from the field and retain finite-boundary terms
methods.principle: Quadratic field-energy integral
steps: Find the total field in every region
Square it with the proper electric or magnetic coefficient and all cross terms
Integrate with the appropriate volume measure
Retain the scalar-potential flux or vector-potential cross-field boundary term for a finite enclosing region
Take the all-space limit only when the boundary contribution vanishes
methods.boundary: Include material response or maintained-source work only under the appropriate energy convention; point self energies may diverge.

methods.title: Interpret or construct oriented field-line diagrams
methods.principle: A single-valued vector field is tangent to its oriented field lines
steps: Identify the actual vector field and its allowed sources or absence of sources
Use local arrows and relative line density to infer direction and relative strength
Superpose field components before constructing the total-field lines
When a formula is supplied, solve the tangent relation between coordinate differentials
Locate cancellations, symmetry axes and limiting behavior
Distinguish field direction from the force or trajectory of a moving particle
methods.boundary: Electric lines may start or end on charges; magnetic lines have no monopole sources in the stated theory. Lines of different component fields may cross; lines of a nonzero single-valued total field do not. A field line is not generally a released-particle trajectory.

methods.title: Find flux through a face by symmetry completion
methods.principle: Total enclosed flux and equal symmetric patches
steps: Complete the geometry so the source is at a symmetry center
Apply Gauss law to the full enclosing surface
Count congruent patches with equal oriented flux
Divide the total flux and restore the requested orientation
methods.boundary: Do not assign a point source on a surface to its enclosed volume without a limiting construction.

methods.title: Relate net closed-surface electric flux to enclosed charge
methods.principle: Gauss law: signed closed flux equals net enclosed charge divided by permittivity
steps: Identify a genuinely closed surface and its outward orientation
Decide which charges lie inside, outside or ambiguously on the boundary
Sum the enclosed signed charges or integrate their density
Use net flux equals enclosed charge over permittivity, or invert it
Distinguish zero net flux from zero field point by point
methods.boundary: No symmetry is required for the net flux relation. A local field value requires an additional symmetry or boundary argument; flux through an open piece alone is not fixed by net enclosed charge.

methods.title: Obtain a field from Gauss law and source symmetry
methods.principle: Closed flux equals enclosed source strength
steps: Establish spherical, cylindrical or plane symmetry
Choose a matching Gaussian surface
Identify constant normal and zero-flux portions
Integrate the enclosed density separately in each region
Solve for the field
Check interface jumps and limiting behavior
methods.boundary: Gauss law is always valid but determines the local field by this recipe only with sufficient symmetry. Boundary conditions at infinity matter for infinite sources.

methods.title: Reconstruct a field or potential from its divergence and curl
methods.principle: Helmholtz or Poisson Green-kernel reconstruction
steps: Write the defining divergence and curl equations
Compare them with a known Green-kernel problem
Map sources and constants while preserving vector products
Include boundary or decay conditions
Write the resulting volume integral
Verify by applying the defining differential operators
methods.boundary: Decay and topology assumptions control whether boundary or harmonic terms can be omitted.

methods.title: Rule out an interior electrostatic extremum or stable equilibrium
methods.principle: Maximum principle for harmonic potentials
steps: Identify a source-free neighborhood
Apply the harmonic mean-value or maximum principle
Exclude a strict interior maximum or minimum
Relate stable test-charge equilibrium to a potential-energy minimum
Examine an explicit escape direction when requested
methods.boundary: A symmetry center can be stationary without being stable. Constrained motion and nonelectrostatic forces change the conclusion.

methods.title: Integrate the field of a continuous charge,mass or prescribed elementary source
methods.principle: Continuous linear superposition with the appropriate established source kernel
steps: Parameterize the source and its charge,mass,moment or phase measure
Write the source-to-observer geometry and the established elementary-source field
Resolve vectors in a common basis and cancel components by symmetry
Integrate the surviving components over the complete source
Check normalization,direction,units and approximation limits
methods.boundary: Derivation of a retarded point field or magnetic moment remains separate. Biot-Savart construction additionally specifies the oriented current-element cross-product kernel.

methods.title: Derive a field equation from its integral kernel
methods.principle: Differentiate a Green kernel distributionally
steps: Write the source convolution and identify the differentiation coordinate
Apply the requested differential operator to the kernel
Include its singular distribution and regular remainder
Sift the source density
Use the divergence theorem for the integral form
State decay and boundary assumptions
When the kernel is retarded,include retarded-time chain derivatives and use source continuity and integration by parts with the stated boundary falloff

methods.title: Solve a separable Laplace boundary-value problem by mode expansion
methods.principle: Separated harmonic modes and boundary matching
steps: Choose coordinates and separate the source-free equation in each region
Retain the zero mode and every regular or decaying branch allowed by the domain
Expand nonconstant boundary data in the angular or transverse orthogonal basis
Match potentials and specified normal derivative jumps
Solve the coefficient equations mode by mode
Reconstruct the potential and required fields or surface densities
methods.boundary: Cartesian sine/hyperbolic, spherical Legendre/power and cylindrical Fourier/power bases are coordinate variants. Multiple regions, charge jumps, nonzero modes at infinity and source sheets must be retained explicitly; they are not optional steps.

methods.title: Prove a spherical mean-value identity from the field equation
methods.principle: Derivative of a surface average and divergence theorem
steps: Parameterize the average over a sphere of variable radius
Differentiate the average while holding angular coordinates fixed
Convert the radial derivative integral to flux
Use the source-free Laplacian or enclosed source term
Integrate in radius and fix the small-radius limit
methods.boundary: Distinguish surface averages from volume averages and do not cross an unaccounted singular source.

methods.title: Construct and test a hypothetical extension of field laws
methods.principle: Symmetry, dimensions, conservation and empirical distinguishability
steps: State the proposed new sources and their units
Identify the existing law or symmetry being changed
Write candidate source and force terms that reduce to the known theory
Check divergence identities and source continuity
Identify any unconstrained coefficients or alternative rules
Propose an observable that would distinguish the alternatives
methods.boundary: A hypothetical-model question does not establish existence of its proposed particles or select a unique extension without additional principles or data.

methods.title: Find far-field behavior from source moments
methods.principle: Ordered inverse-distance expansion of the potential kernel
steps: Choose the origin and far-field parameter
Calculate the monopole and successive signed source moments using symmetry
Retain enough orders to meet the request or reach the first nonzero contribution
Reconstruct angular dependence in the appropriate basis
Differentiate for the requested field or force
Check validity and whether higher moments vanish exactly
methods.boundary: Far-field truncation does not prove an exact all-distance result without showing the other allowed moments vanish.

methods.title: Derive or transform Cartesian multipole tensors
methods.principle: Taylor expansion and symmetric trace-free moments
steps: Expand the inverse-distance kernel in Cartesian components
Contract the source-coordinate powers with observation-direction factors
Separate traces to define the stated multipole convention
Integrate each tensor component
For an origin shift expand translated source coordinates
Identify the lower moments that control translation dependence
methods.boundary: Numerical factors vary with tensor conventions. Dipole origin independence requires zero monopole; quadrupole origin independence requires zero monopole and dipole.

methods.title: Sum or integrate the scalar potential of a prescribed source
methods.principle: Superposition of inverse-distance potentials
steps: Set a common permissible reference
Express the source-to-observation distance
Write the signed source element and geometric measure
Sum or integrate the scalar kernel
Treat distinct geometric regions and absolute-value branches
Differentiate only coordinates whose dependence is known when a field is requested
methods.boundary: Knowing a potential only along one line does not determine its transverse gradient.

methods.title: Find conductor charge totals with an auxiliary electrostatic problem
methods.principle: Reciprocal source-potential integrals
steps: Choose an auxiliary configuration with known conductor potentials and simple interior potential
Apply reciprocity to actual and auxiliary configurations
Replace conductor integrals by constant potential times total charge
Include discrete interior charges with their auxiliary potential values
Solve for the requested conductor total
Repeat auxiliary boundary choices when several totals are required
methods.boundary: This yields total induced charge without determining its local surface density.

methods.title: Validate a candidate boundary-value solution and invoke uniqueness
methods.principle: Field equation, interfaces, boundary conditions and uniqueness
steps: Check the differential source equation in every open region
Verify all prescribed potential and flux conditions including interfaces
Check singular sources and behavior at infinity
Verify conductor charges or potentials as specified
Apply the appropriate uniqueness theorem
Identify exactly which condition fails for altered geometry
methods.boundary: Matching one boundary is insufficient, and the uniqueness theorem cannot fix a candidate that violates another interface.

methods.title: Compute continuous-source self energy from density and potential
methods.principle: Half the integral of source density times total potential
steps: Obtain the scalar or vector potential with its fixed reference and gauge
Choose the volume, surface or line source measure
Integrate one half of rho V or current density dot A as appropriate
Keep self and interaction conventions explicit
Check sign, units and scaling
methods.boundary: Point self energies can diverge. This energy of assembled sources differs from adding a fixed test object or moving a fixed dipole with maintained external currents.

methods.title: Add known fields or potentials using linearity and symmetry
methods.principle: Linear superposition of fields
steps: Specify each source position and signed strength
Write each known elementary field or potential at the observation point with its consistent reference
Express vector components in one basis;sum scalar potentials without assigning vector directions
Use symmetry or subtract a missing source
Sum the surviving components
Check the resulting magnitude and direction
methods.boundary: A geometrical symmetry argument must apply to the whole source configuration or to explicitly superposed pieces.

methods.title: Find the differential field relative to an accelerating origin
methods.principle: Subtract the reference-point field and expand in separation
steps: Write the source-to-body and source-to-origin vectors
Subtract their inverse-square accelerations
Expand consistently in the small body-to-source distance ratio
Retain the requested order and direction
Compare with the dominant local field
methods.boundary: Parallel and transverse displacements are components of the same differential-field procedure, not separate problem types.

methods.title: Prove uniqueness by an energy integral for the difference field
methods.principle: Green identity and positivity of the squared gradient
steps: Subtract two proposed solutions with the same sources
Form the homogeneous equation and boundary data
Integrate the squared difference gradient using Green identity
Show each boundary contribution vanishes using potential, normal derivative or conductor charge constraints
Infer a constant potential difference
Fix the constant when a Dirichlet reference exists
methods.boundary: All-Neumann data determine potential only up to a constant and require compatibility for existence. Uniqueness is not an existence proof.

methods.title: Relate steady fluid speed, pressure and height by Bernoulli energy balance
methods.principle: Pressure work, gravitational energy and kinetic energy balance along a streamline
steps: Choose two locations on the same steady-flow path
Write pressure plus one-half density times speed squared plus density*g*height at both points
Apply boundary pressures and use continuity for any non-negligible reservoir speed
Include a stated pump input or loss term only when supplied
Solve the requested speed, pressure or stopping level and select the physically accessible branch
Check the incompressible, negligible-viscosity and steady-flow approximations
methods.boundary: Gas compression setting a reservoir pressure is an additional state-relation step. An inviscid ideal flow result does not establish a real discharge rate without outlet area and losses.

methods.title: Balance weight against displaced-fluid buoyancy
methods.principle: Archimedes force and static vertical force balance
steps: Identify displaced external-fluid volume
Calculate its weight
Include the object, payload and internal-fluid masses separately
Impose the supported-weight condition
Use an equation of state if a fluid density is unknown
For a qualitative convection question compare parcel and surrounding densities to decide whether the parcel sinks or rises; retain density extrema and phase assumptions
methods.boundary: A hot-air balloon is open to ambient pressure; equal pressure does not imply equal density.

methods.title: Find buoyancy and a tether direction in an accelerated fluid
methods.principle: Hydrostatic pressure gradient in effective gravity
steps: Combine gravity and frame acceleration into effective gravity
Obtain the pressure-gradient direction
Integrate displaced-fluid pressure force or use Archimedes force opposite effective gravity
Add the object effective weight and tether force
Determine the equilibrium direction and angle

methods.title: Find an equilibrium free-fluid surface from potential
methods.principle: Constant total potential at uniform surface pressure
steps: Construct the gravitational and inertial or tidal potentials
Evaluate or expand them at a general surface point
Set their sum equal to a reference surface value
Solve for the surface height or shape
Apply the stated small-height and geometry approximations
methods.boundary: A tidal quadrupole requires keeping second-order distance terms even though its force is first order in displacement.

methods.title: Find fluid circulation induced by reorienting a thin ring
methods.principle: Conservation of inertial circulation for an ideal fluid
steps: Relate inertial circulation to fluid speed relative to the ring and projected Earth rotation
Identify the initial ring normal and zero relative flow
Reverse the ring normal
Conserve circulation neglecting viscous tangential impulse during the flip
Solve the resulting relative flow speed
methods.boundary: The ring changes orientation, so conservation of a fixed-axis angular-momentum component is not an automatic substitute for the circulation argument.

methods.title: Find stratification from hydrostatic balance and an equation of state
methods.principle: dP/dz=-rho g
steps: Balance forces on a thin horizontal slab
Express density using the stated equation of state
Insert the temperature or other profile assumption
Integrate with the boundary pressure
Obtain density and check the scale height and validity region
methods.boundary: An isothermal exponential atmosphere and an adiabatic parcel are different thermodynamic constraints.

methods.title: Compute the minimum environmental entropy and heat required for erasure
methods.principle: Logical state compression must be compensated outside the erased memory
steps: Count unknown bits using the specified storage-unit convention
Compute their initial information entropy and the erased-state reduction
Apply nondecrease of total entropy to bound environmental entropy gain
Multiply by reservoir temperature to bound dumped heat
Distinguish the reversible-limit bound from actual device dissipation
methods.boundary: The k log 2 per bit value assumes initially unknown equally likely independent bits. At the reversible limit the environment gain compensates memory loss, so total entropy production can approach zero.

methods.title: Compare electron microscope signal paths
methods.principle: Transmission and surface-scanning instruments form images from different electron signals
steps: Trace the source, accelerated beam and focusing path
Identify whether the specimen is traversed or scanned at its surface
Identify transmitted, secondary or backscattered signals
Relate the signal to sample thickness and information recovered
Explain the vacuum requirement from unwanted scattering
methods.boundary: Resolution and magnification are different properties; no current commercial specification is required by this historical textbook comparison.

methods.title: Determine a magnetostatic field with an Amperian loop
methods.principle: Circulation equals permeability times enclosed current
steps: Use source symmetries to establish field direction and constancy
Choose a loop with calculable parallel and zero contributions
Integrate the signed enclosed current
Solve separately in each source region
Set any exterior constant using a boundary condition
Check surface-current jumps
methods.boundary: The integral law alone does not determine a general nonsymmetric local field; arbitrary solenoid cross sections require a separate field-direction argument.

methods.title: Calculate a steady-current field by direct integration
methods.principle: Biot-Savart superposition
steps: Parameterize the current and source-to-observer displacement
Express source vectors in a common basis
Evaluate the current-element cross displacement kernel
Use symmetry to cancel components
Integrate over the full line, sheet or volume or over known elementary loops
Check direction and appropriate limiting cases
methods.boundary: An axis-only formula cannot be used unchanged off axis. Steady currents must be closed or have an explicitly modeled return path at infinity.

methods.title: Relate magnetic and vector-potential jumps to a sheet current
methods.principle: Normal B continuity and tangential B jump
steps: Choose one interface normal
Evaluate the one-sided magnetic fields
Compare their difference with permeability times sheet current cross normal
In the specified regular Coulomb gauge check vector-potential continuity
Take its normal derivative jump and compare with minus permeability times sheet current
Retain tangential derivatives and gauge assumptions
methods.boundary: Vector-potential continuity statements here assume the stated gauge and ordinary sheet currents, not arbitrary discontinuous gauge transformations.

methods.title: Replace prescribed magnetization by bound currents
methods.principle: Volume curl and surface cross-normal magnetization
steps: Identify material regions and every outward normal
Calculate curl M within each region
Calculate M cross outward normal on each surface
Combine one-sided interface contributions
Keep singular current terms when M is discontinuous
Check current conservation and integrated cancellation where required
methods.boundary: Curl-free interior magnetization can still have surface current. Uniform direction and azimuthal direction are different vector fields.
