methods.title: Prove magnetic-field uniqueness with a curl-energy identity
methods.principle: Positive integral of the squared difference curl
steps: Subtract two fields with the same current density
Choose their vector-potential difference
Apply the curl integration-by-parts identity
Eliminate the volume source term and the specified boundary difference
Infer zero integral of difference B squared
Conclude field uniqueness while preserving potential gauge freedom
methods.boundary: Field uniqueness does not imply uniqueness of the vector potential.

methods.title: Find the magnetic field of a moving charge or short current element
methods.principle: The same vector kernel uses q v for a moving point charge and I dl for a short current segment
steps: Form the displacement from the source to the field point
Normalize the displacement or retain its cubed length in the denominator

methods.title: Find force on line, surface or volume currents

Exclude the selected object self contribution or justify internal-force cancellation
Parameterize the oriented line, surface or volume current
Take the current cross field product
Integrate each force component
Average the two one-sided fields for an ideal current sheet

Insert it into the current-element force integral
Show the uniform-field term cancels around a closed loop
Evaluate first moments of oriented line elements using area or component identities
Use divergence B=0 to simplify
Identify current times vector area and recover the gradient force

methods.title: Find magnetic moments of closed or distributed currents

Compute each signed current and oriented area or the equivalent moment integral
Sum or integrate contributions
Check independence from the origin for a localized steady current
Insert the resulting moment into a far-field potential or field if requested
Distinguish exact dipole sources from leading far-field approximations

methods.title: Choose a field-history path to change remanent magnetization
methods.principle: Domain response depends on the prior applied field

Distinguish zero applied field from zero magnetization
Follow reversed and alternating field excursions
Reduce their amplitude to shrink the remanent domain imbalance
End with zero field and near-zero net magnetization
State why simply switching off the initial field does not suffice

methods.principle: Biot-Savart force and closed-loop total derivatives

Expand the vector triple product
Show the closed-loop total-derivative term vanishes
Interchange the two loop labels in the remaining double integral
Compare signs to obtain force antisymmetry

methods.title: Match fields at a magnetic-material interface
methods.principle: Continuous normal B and free-current tangential H jump

Apply zero normal B jump
Set the tangential H jump from the free sheet current
Substitute each medium permeability or fixed magnetization
Solve the component or angle relation
Recover bound-current effects without counting them as free current

Apply the stated pairing or unpaired-moment model
Determine whether a permanent moment can give a paramagnetic response
Otherwise retain the induced diamagnetic contribution
Note stated material exceptions and the limits of the elementary model

methods.title: Explain current transport in the type-II mixed state

Distinguish normal vortex cores from the connected superconducting material
Determine whether current can flow through the superconducting regions
State the pinned-vortex and critical-current assumptions behind zero resistance
Distinguish dissipative moving vortices from a static mixed-state picture

methods.title: Solve an initial-value differential equation by a power series
methods.principle: Coefficient matching
steps: Insert an unknown power series and its derivatives
Match coefficients of equal powers
Obtain and iterate the recurrence from the initial coefficient
Identify the summed function and domain
methods.boundary: No eigenvalue termination condition is present; retain separately from quantizing a polynomial eigenproblem.

methods.title: Prove an identity by multiplying convergent power series
methods.principle: Cauchy product and coefficient matching
steps: Write both power series
Group product terms by total degree
Evaluate each finite coefficient sum
Use the binomial theorem or the required coefficient identity
Recognize the target series and state convergence assumptions

methods.title: Transform an operator equation or spectrum by similarity
methods.principle: Invertible change of basis
steps: Insert the similarity definitions with a consistent order
Cancel adjacent inverse matrices in products
Transform the eigenvector or equation correspondingly
Identify preserved eigenvalues, products or commutators
methods.boundary: Invertibility alone preserves algebra and spectrum; unitarity is additionally needed for the unchanged Euclidean inner product.

methods.title: Sum successive linear-response corrections and test convergence
methods.principle: Geometric or Neumann series of a linear feedback map
steps: Write the first response to the uncorrected input
Apply the same response map repeatedly
Identify the ratio or linear operator power
Sum the convergent series
State its convergence domain
Compare the algebraic fixed-point solution outside that domain without calling the divergent iteration convergent
methods.boundary: An algebraic continuation of a rational result does not make the original series converge.

methods.title: Prove cyclic trace and its similarity invariance
methods.principle: Finite component sums
steps: Write the trace of the product as indexed sums
Relabel dummy indices cyclically
Apply the cyclic identity to cancel an inverse pair if present
In an eigenbasis or triangular form read the sum of eigenvalues
methods.boundary: Cyclic permutation does not authorize arbitrary reordering. Use triangularization rather than assume every arbitrary matrix is unitarily diagonalizable.

methods.title: Prove transpose or adjoint reversal of a matrix product
methods.principle: Component-index contraction
steps: Write one entry of the product and transpose it
Reverse the dummy-index order
Identify the product of individually transposed factors in reverse order
Include complex conjugation only for an adjoint
Check dimensions

methods.title: Construct a unitary matrix with specified entry properties
methods.principle: Orthonormal columns
steps: Choose normalized mutually orthogonal complex columns
Insert phases satisfying the requested real/imaginary entry condition
Assemble the columns into a matrix
Verify the conjugate-transpose product is identity

methods.title: Convert physical quantities between stated units
methods.principle: Multiply by unit ratios equal to one
steps: Write the quantity with its complete units
Insert the energy, length, mass or time conversion ratios
Retain powers of c or other dimensional constants
Cancel units explicitly
Evaluate in the requested system

methods.title: Verify a curl-gradient or divergence-curl identity
methods.principle: Commuting mixed partial derivatives
steps: Expand the vector derivatives in Cartesian components
Pair oppositely signed mixed derivatives
Cancel them for smooth single-valued fields
Identify singularities or excluded domains where the local identity does not settle a global integral

methods.title: Derive a curvilinear area or volume element
methods.principle: Local Jacobian or metric scale factors
steps: Write the coordinate-to-Cartesian mapping
Find local basis derivative lengths or the Jacobian determinant
Multiply independent infinitesimal edge factors
Take the absolute volume factor
State coordinate ranges and singular sets

methods.title: Integrate a prescribed density or scalar over a volume
methods.principle: Iterated integration with the geometric measure
steps: Describe the domain and bounds
Choose coordinates adapted to its geometry
Include the volume Jacobian
Perform the nested integrals
Check dimensions and the sign or total normalization

methods.title: Report precision and significant figures consistently
methods.principle: A result cannot claim more measurement resolution than its inputs
steps: Identify stated input resolution and exact constants
Calculate with guard digits
Use decimal-place limits for sums and significant-figure limits for products
Round the final quantity and express units
Compare with a known reference using signed or absolute fractional error as requested
methods.boundary: Rounding rules do not by themselves propagate a probability distribution of experimental errors.

methods.title: Assess a measurement standard or a resolution-limited measurement scheme
methods.principle: Reproducibility and stability make a physical comparison meaningful
steps: Identify the measured quantity and the proposed reference process
Relate the measured signal to the target quantity
Check drift, resolution and reproducibility
Use repeated units or an accumulated measurement when one unit is below resolution
Explain systematic bias versus repeatability
methods.boundary: Conceptual measurement design is not a quantum uncertainty calculation.

methods.title: Propagate stated measurement uncertainties through a formula
methods.principle: Small changes follow partial derivatives of the measured function
steps: Write the derived quantity in terms of measured inputs
Differentiate with respect to each input
Combine absolute contributions for a worst-case bound or covariance terms for statistical uncertainty
Evaluate the requested absolute and fractional uncertainties
State the approximation order and interpretation of each uncertainty
methods.boundary: Do not replace a requested worst-case sum by quadrature without an independent-error probabilistic assumption.

methods.title: Determine rotation changes from conserved angular momentum
methods.principle: Zero external torque about a specified axis
steps: Choose the axis and show the external torque or angular impulse vanishes
Write the initial angular momentum
Express the final angular momentum using the changed radius, mass or moment of inertia
Equate the two values
Solve for angular speed and check scaling
If requested,compare initial and final kinetic energies after the angular speeds are known;angular conservation alone does not imply energy conservation
methods.boundary: Matter added to the system contributes its incoming angular momentum, which is zero only under the stated condition.

methods.title: Integrate torque to find acquired angular momentum
methods.principle: Time derivative of angular momentum equals torque
steps: Choose a fixed torque origin or axis
Write position cross the external force
Express the torque along the trajectory
Change the integration variable if it removes unknown time dependence
Integrate from the initial to final state
Relate the resulting angular momentum to the outgoing direction
methods.boundary: Zero final angular momentum does not mean the torque vanished throughout the motion. Electromagnetic transfer uses the actual distributed torque;spinning charged bodies can retain final field angular momentum,so conservation of total momentum does not replace a requested torque integral.

methods.title: Reduce constrained motion to arclength
methods.principle: Unit tangent and tangential Newton equation
steps: Parameterize the curve by arclength
Differentiate position to show that speed is the magnitude of the arclength rate
Project acceleration and force onto the unit tangent
Use the chain rule to identify minus the potential derivative along the curve
Form the one-dimensional motion equation

methods.title: Derive the constant-area-rate law
methods.principle: Angular momentum and infinitesimal swept triangle
steps: Resolve velocity into radial and transverse components
Form position cross momentum
Write the infinitesimal swept area from the transverse displacement
Divide by elapsed time and relate to angular momentum
Invoke zero central torque for constancy

methods.title: Find the threshold to cross a potential barrier
methods.principle: Initial energy compared with an accessible maximum
steps: Find the release energy from the stated initial position and speed
Locate the next intervening potential maximum in the direction of motion
Equate its height to the release energy at threshold
Solve the simultaneous stationary-point and energy equations
Check accessibility and separate the threshold from merely having an equilibrium

methods.title: Solve a central-force orbit in inverse-radius coordinates
methods.principle: Angular momentum eliminates time and gives the Binet equation
steps: Set u=1/r and replace time derivatives using angular momentum
Insert the specified signed force law
Solve the resulting equation for u(phi)
Fit constants or distinguish characteristic-root regimes
Restrict to positive u and interpret turning points or singular ends
Convert back to r(phi)
methods.boundary: An attractive inverse-cube correction can change oscillatory roots to real exponential roots; this is not a Kepler conic with a changed eccentricity alone.

methods.title: Verify and use a canonical coordinate transformation
methods.principle: Chain rule preserves Hamilton equations
steps: Specify the forward and inverse phase-coordinate maps and their domains
Differentiate the transformed Hamiltonian and new variables
Substitute the original Hamilton equations
Check the new canonical pair equations
Simplify the transformed Hamiltonian
Integrate and transform back when requested
methods.boundary: Polar phase coordinates require a local angle chart and are singular at zero amplitude.

methods.title: Prove planarity and angular conservation for a central force
methods.principle: Vanishing position-cross-force torque
steps: Choose the force center as origin
Differentiate position cross momentum
Use the radial force direction to set torque to zero
If planarity is requested,use the constant nonzero angular-momentum vector as a fixed plane normal
Treat zero-angular-momentum radial motion separately

methods.title: Relate a circular orbit to its radial force or energy
methods.principle: Centripetal acceleration and radial force
steps: Identify the inward radial component of force
Differentiate a supplied radial potential when needed
Equate inward force to m*v_transverse squared/r,or p_transverse*v_transverse/r for a relativistic fixed-speed magnetic orbit
Solve for speed, tension or kinetic energy
Substitute the given radial power law or orbit constraint
Use circumference and speed to obtain period or frequency if requested; distinguish the circular transverse speed from any longitudinal drift
For a helical magnetic orbit retain the independent longitudinal drift;pitch is longitudinal speed times gyroperiod
For a finite magnetic region intersect the circular arc with its actual boundary before applying a small-angle limit
methods.boundary: This is a circular-orbit relation, not the quantum commutator proof of the virial theorem.

methods.title: Integrate a continuous center of mass
methods.principle: First spatial moment divided by total mass
steps: Use symmetry to identify zero components
Choose coordinates and the correct length, area or volume measure
Express the mass density and its support
Integrate each required position component times mass density
Divide by the total mass and check the result lies in the geometric convex hull
For a center of gravity in a parallel but nonuniform gravitational field,replace mass weighting by local weight weighting
methods.boundary: Center of mass and center of gravity coincide in a uniform gravitational field. A general nonparallel field need not admit one point representing all gravitational force and torque.

methods.title: Find a discrete or composite center of mass
methods.principle: Mass-weighted position average
steps: Choose a common coordinate origin
List each mass and position
Sum mass times position componentwise
Divide by total mass
Use symmetry and limiting mass ratios to check the location
methods.boundary: Computing a continuous mass distribution needs an explicit integration measure.

methods.title: Track center-of-mass motion under external forces
methods.principle: Total mass times CM acceleration equals external force
steps: Identify the full material system and its net external forces
Cancel internal interactions
Integrate the CM motion independently of fragmentation
Relate simultaneous fragment positions to the CM by mass weighting
Reassess the external forces after contact or landing
methods.boundary: Positions at different times cannot be averaged as if simultaneous, and ground impulses change subsequent CM motion.

methods.title: Prove center-of-mass regrouping identities
methods.principle: Linearity of mass-weighted sums
steps: Expand the center-of-mass definition
Partition the particle sum into the specified subsystems or subtract the chosen center
Recognize each subsystem mass times its own center
Simplify the weighted sums
Interpret the result geometrically

methods.title: Prove the torque law about an accelerating center of mass
methods.principle: Vanishing first mass moment in CM coordinates
steps: Subtract the CM coordinate from every particle position
Prove the mass-weighted relative-position sum vanishes
Differentiate angular momentum about that moving point
Cancel translation and acceleration terms using the zero first moment
Cancel internal central torques
Retain the external torque about the CM

methods.title: Transform two-body expressions to center-of-mass and relative coordinates
methods.principle: Mass-weighted linear coordinate transformation
steps: Write the center-of-mass and relative coordinates and their inverse
Write the corresponding momenta
Substitute into the specified quadratic or bilinear expression
Cancel mixed terms and identify total and reduced masses

methods.title: Solve connected masses and pulleys using Newton equations
methods.principle: Force and torque balances with length constraints
steps: Draw separate free-body diagrams
Write each translational force equation
Add the pulley torque equation when its inertia is nonzero
Use string-length and no-slip acceleration constraints
Eliminate tensions and solve for the common acceleration
methods.boundary: A massive pulley generally has unequal tensions on its two sides.

methods.title: Verify a proposed conserved quantity from the equations of motion
methods.principle: Differentiate the proposed invariant and substitute the actual dynamical equations
steps: Differentiate the scalar,vector or quadratic expression along the motion
Include moving-basis derivatives or use the specified body-frame component equations consistently
Substitute every force or component derivative from the given equations of motion
Collect products and apply the required algebraic,vector or inertia identities
Establish that the derivative vanishes under the stated assumptions
Use the resulting invariant and initial data for any requested reduction
methods.boundary: The invariant must hold for the actual force and coordinate convention. Opposite pair forces alone do not imply zero torque;velocity-dependent forces need not be central.

methods.title: Solve constant-acceleration motion and crossing constraints
methods.principle: A coordinate is quadratic in time when its second derivative is constant
steps: Choose signed Cartesian components or one fixed-axis angular coordinate
Write rate=initial_rate+acceleration*time and coordinate=initial_coordinate+initial_rate*time+acceleration*time squared/2
Use the specified endpoint, crossing or stopping condition to eliminate unknowns
Select physical time roots and carry final states between distinct constant-acceleration stages
Convert units and distinguish signed displacement from total path length
methods.boundary: Fixed-axis angular motion uses the same steps after x,v,a are replaced by theta,omega,alpha. It does not cover changing-axis rotation, variable acceleration, or an added optimization over trajectories.

methods.title: Calculate work by constant forces on a specified displacement
methods.principle: Each force contributes its dot product with the displacement of its point of application
steps: Identify the body or subsystem and the displacement relevant to each force
Resolve the constant force and displacement in common axes or find their included angle
Calculate each signed force-displacement dot product
Sum contributions only for the requested system
Compare paths or frames using their actual displacements
methods.boundary: A nonzero force can do zero work. Third-law force equality alone does not prove equal and opposite work unless the application-point displacements also agree. Constant-direction gravity work depends only on height change.

methods.title: Derive stationary action with ideal constraints
methods.principle: Newton equations and zero constraint virtual work
steps: Vary a kinematically admissible path with fixed endpoints
Integrate kinetic variation by parts
Replace acceleration with applied plus constraint forces
Cancel conservative force variation
Sum constraint virtual work over coupled particles
Use ideality to show vanishing first variation
methods.boundary: Zero fixed-time virtual work does not imply zero actual work for a moving constraint.

methods.title: Construct potential energy in a constrained coordinate
methods.principle: Geometry of heights and spring extensions
steps: Choose the independent coordinate
Use fixed lengths, rolling geometry or other constraints to express each height and extension
Sum gravitational and elastic potentials
State the physically accessible coordinate interval
Choose an irrelevant additive constant conveniently

methods.title: Match constrained and free motion at loss of contact
methods.principle: Unilateral normal-force condition and continuous position/velocity
steps: Solve motion while contact is maintained
Compute the required normal reaction
Find its first zero and check whether the event is reached
Release the constraint when continued contact would require negative normal force
Match position and velocity into free motion
Stop or change phase at subsequent contact
methods.boundary: Initial contact cannot be discarded merely because later motion admits a center-of-mass decomposition.

methods.title: Compute kinetic energy of a distributed moving body
methods.principle: Integral of one-half speed squared over mass
steps: Choose a material coordinate and mass element
Express the local velocity in terms of the generalized velocity
Integrate local kinetic energy
Combine with the remaining lumped masses or rotational contributions
Interpret the resulting effective inertia

methods.title: Derive first-order Coriolis corrections to free fall
methods.principle: Successive approximation in a small rotation rate
steps: Resolve angular velocity into local axes
Solve the zero-rotation trajectory
Insert its velocity into the rotation-dependent acceleration
Integrate twice with zero correction to initial data
Drop second-order terms
State the time and distance regime of validity

methods.title: Solve force balances with static or sliding contact friction
methods.principle: Static friction supplies the required tangential force up to its limiting magnitude; sliding friction opposes relative slip
steps: Draw each body free of its contacts and resolve the normal direction first
Determine whether each contact sticks, is impending slip, or slides relative to the other surface
For sticking solve for the required friction and test its magnitude against mu-static times normal force
For sliding use mu-kinetic times normal force in the direction opposing relative slip
Combine tangential force equations with the relevant common-motion or rope constraint
Solve for acceleration, applied force or the limiting parameter and check normal and tension positivity
Change the contact branch if a no-slip, taut-rope or maintained-contact assumption fails
methods.boundary: Static friction is not generally its limiting value and can accelerate a body. Pulling or pushing at an angle changes the normal force. Reversed motion changes kinetic-friction sign; negative calculated tension means a rope constraint cannot hold.

methods.title: Resolve curved-path acceleration into speed change and turning
methods.principle: Tangential acceleration is the speed derivative and inward normal acceleration is speed squared over curvature radius
steps: Identify the local tangent and inward normal to the path
Determine whether speed is increasing, decreasing or momentarily stationary
Use a tangential component dv/dt and a normal component v squared over radius
Relate circular speed, radius, angular rate and period when applicable
Combine components or compare scalings as requested
methods.boundary: This is kinematics with known speed or period. Deriving that speed from force balance is an additional dynamics task. Radius means distance from the rotation axis, not automatically a string length.

methods.title: Build a reduced effective potential from conserved momenta
methods.principle: Eliminate cyclic velocities in the conserved total energy
steps: Compute or use the cyclic conjugate momenta
Solve them for the corresponding velocities
Substitute into the total energy
Separate the remaining kinetic term from its effective potential
Retain constants and endpoint-domain restrictions
methods.boundary: Substitution here is into energy, not naive substitution into the Lagrangian.

methods.title: Reduce motion using a cyclic generalized coordinate
methods.principle: Conservation of conjugate momentum
steps: Identify an absent coordinate in L
Compute and conserve its conjugate momentum
Solve that relation for its velocity
Substitute into the other equations of motion
Interpret the conserved quantity and resulting reduced dynamics
methods.boundary: Substituting the conserved velocity into L without a Routh transformation can give an incorrect reduced equation.

methods.title: Infer decay, period and quality factor of an underdamped oscillator
methods.principle: Exponential envelope and damped angular frequency
steps: Relate natural and damped frequencies through the damping constant
Relate successive peak heights or a decay time through the exponential envelope
Solve the measured-period and decay equations
Convert between cycle count and elapsed time
Calculate the requested quality factor or amplitude ratio
methods.boundary: A decay time for amplitude is twice the energy decay time; keep the definition supplied by the source.

methods.title: Integrate torque from forces on a distributed body
methods.principle: Total torque is the integral of position cross local force
steps: Parameterize the material or source elements and their positions relative to the torque origin
Express each local velocity and force
Form the torque element
Use symmetry and integrate over the body
Determine magnitude and direction
methods.boundary: For Coriolis forcing the velocity varies over the spinning body and cannot be replaced by the center velocity.

methods.title: Compare drag with another force and identify the relevant regime
methods.principle: Dimensionless force ratio
steps: Write the competing force laws with consistent units and geometry
Use a stated terminal balance to eliminate an unknown drag coefficient if helpful
Form their dimensionless ratio
Solve equality for a crossover scale if requested
Compare the ratio with unity and state which force can be neglected
methods.boundary: A trajectory under drag additionally requires solving its equation of motion.

methods.title: Find a sinusoidal steady response and its transient motion
methods.principle: Complex particular solution plus homogeneous response
steps: Replace the sinusoidal force by its complex exponential
Divide by the complex response denominator
Determine magnitude and quadrant-correct phase
Take the real part
Add the correct homogeneous solution when initial conditions are requested
Match initial data and distinguish transient from steady frequencies

methods.title: Analyze effective radial force and turning points
methods.principle: Centrifugal term and radial energy balance
steps: Add the angular-momentum barrier to the interaction potential
Differentiate for the effective force or set effective potential equal to energy for turning radii
Solve the sign condition or roots
Select the physical radial domain

methods.title: Combine momentum and kinetic-energy conservation in a collision
methods.principle: Isolated elastic collision
steps: Write vector momentum conservation
Write scalar kinetic-energy conservation
Eliminate the known initial or final velocities
Solve the remaining equations or infer an angle from their dot products
Select physical collision branches

methods.title: Relate initial and final motion using mechanical energy and stated work
methods.principle: Work-energy balance for the selected system
steps: Identify kinetic and potential energy terms at each specified state
Include work by forces outside the chosen conservative system when present
Equate final energy to initial energy plus that work
Impose geometric or event constraints
Solve and select physically permitted speeds or positions
methods.boundary: Use only simultaneous or asymptotic states justified by the problem; do not assume conservation when the potential depends explicitly on time. A supplied quantum energy eigenvalue also equals mean kinetic plus mean potential energy; subtracting the known mean potential is energy bookkeeping,not a classical trajectory claim.

methods.title: Derive mechanical-energy change or conservation from the motion equation
methods.principle: d(K+U)/dt equals explicit potential-time change plus nonconservative power
steps: Differentiate kinetic energy and the stated position-and-time potential along the trajectory
Use the fixed-time potential gradient for the conservative force
Substitute the actual translational or rotational equation of motion
Cancel conservative force-velocity terms and retain both explicit partial U/partial t and any driving or resistive power
Integrate or average only when requested
Identify a first integral only when the remaining energy-change rate vanishes on the physical domain
methods.boundary: An instantaneous force equal to minus the potential gradient does not imply conserved mechanical energy when the potential depends explicitly on time. A formal unwrapped angular work potential need not be single-valued on the physical configuration space.

methods.title: Relate useful output and losses to an input energy reservoir
methods.principle: Efficiency is useful output divided by supplied energy
steps: Identify the available input energy and the useful destination,which may be heat or mechanical work
Use useful output equal to the stated efficiency or retained fraction times supplied energy
Solve for input,output or loss with the actual energy-flow signs
Convert energy to fuel or food mass using the stated energy per mass,and to volume using density when requested
Preserve the destination of every energy portion and distinguish reservoir efficiency from a thermodynamic maximum

methods.title: Derive an equation of motion by differentiating energy
methods.principle: Conserved kinetic plus potential energy
steps: Express all kinetic terms using one coordinate and its speed
Express potential in the same coordinate
Differentiate the conserved total energy
Factor the coordinate velocity
Obtain the motion equation by continuity also at isolated turning points
Include coordinate-dependent kinetic factors when present

methods.title: Prove conservation of a many-particle mechanical energy
methods.principle: Particle work-energy equations and the total potential differential
steps: Write the work-energy theorem for each particle
Sum all kinetic-energy changes
Express each force as the appropriate gradient of the total potential
Combine the coordinate differentials into minus the total potential change
Conclude constancy of total energy when there is no explicit time dependence

methods.title: Find equilibrium and small oscillations from equations of motion
methods.principle: Linearized acceleration near an equilibrium
steps: Set velocities and accelerations to their equilibrium values
Solve the equilibrium condition in the allowed domain
Expand displacement and velocity terms to first order
Read the linear restoring coefficient or coupled stiffness equations
Determine stability and oscillation frequency
State limitations at a zero restoring coefficient
methods.boundary: Do not infer strict instability or a nonzero oscillation frequency when the linear restoring term vanishes.

methods.title: Express rotation vectors in Euler-angle coordinates
methods.principle: Successive rotations and angular-velocity vector addition
steps: State the source Euler-angle convention and order
Express intermediate axes in the requested final basis
Sum the three instantaneous angular-velocity contributions
Project onto body or space axes
Use the principal moments to construct angular momentum or kinetic energy
methods.boundary: Different textbook Euler-angle conventions must be transformed explicitly rather than equated symbol by symbol.

methods.title: Solve Euler equations for an axisymmetric rigid body
methods.principle: Two equal principal moments reduce transverse motion to a phase
steps: Use the symmetry-axis Euler equation to find axial spin
Combine transverse components into one complex variable
Integrate its phase coefficient, allowing time-dependent axial spin
Fit the initial transverse components
Interpret constant amplitude and body-frame precession
methods.boundary: A constant axial torque gives a linearly changing spin and a quadratic accumulated phase, not constant-frequency free precession.

methods.title: Derive fixed-axis rotational motion from torque
methods.principle: Angular-momentum derivative about a fixed pivot
steps: Choose the fixed axis and signed angle
Calculate the applied torque using its lever arm
Use the axial dL/dt=torque law;for constant inertia it reduces to I times angular acceleration,while changing inertia also contributes I-dot times angular velocity
Include specified reaction or drive terms
Interpret the resulting scalar rotational equation
methods.boundary: An axis fixed in direction through the center of mass can be used for the corresponding CM torque equation. During a change of mass distribution,torque=I*alpha alone is incomplete;compare accelerations before and after rearrangement only with their respective inertias.

methods.title: Relate body-frame and space-frame free-precession rates
methods.principle: Angular-velocity addition and the inertia relation
steps: Identify the coplanar symmetry axis, angular velocity and angular momentum
Add relative rotation vectors or compare components perpendicular to the symmetry axis
Use L=I omega to relate their angles
Express the space rate as L divided by the transverse moment
Distinguish that rate from the body-frame wobble

methods.title: Match a periodic physical drive to a natural oscillation
methods.principle: Drive repetition frequency equals the resonant scale
steps: Infer stiffness or the natural oscillation frequency from the supplied static data
Express the imposed event frequency using speed and spatial spacing
Equate drive and natural frequencies at the stated level of approximation
Solve for the speed or spacing
Check units and distinguish angular from ordinary frequency

methods.title: Test a classical law under a Galilean change of frame
methods.principle: Constant-velocity coordinate transformation
steps: Write transformed positions and velocities
Differentiate when accelerations are involved
Transform the proposed force or momentum equation
Cancel invariant terms
Identify the condition needed for the same law in every frame
methods.boundary: This assumes the classical force model used in the question; arbitrary velocity-dependent force laws need not be Galilean invariant.

methods.title: Find slow precession caused by a weak transverse torque
methods.principle: Torque changes angular-momentum direction
steps: Determine spin angular momentum along the symmetry axis
Calculate the applied torque and its direction
Equate it to precession angular velocity cross angular momentum
Solve the precession rate
Check the rapid-spin weak-torque assumption
methods.boundary: This torque-driven precession is not torque-free Euler wobble.

methods.title: Construct a Hamiltonian from a regular Lagrangian
methods.principle: Legendre transformation of velocities into canonical momenta
steps: Express the inertial kinetic and potential terms in the chosen coordinates
Differentiate L with respect to each velocity
Invert the momentum-velocity relations
Form sum p qdot minus L
Express the result entirely in coordinates, momenta and time
Compare with physical energy only when the coordinate and potential conditions justify it
methods.boundary: Time-dependent coordinates or velocity-dependent potentials require the Legendre transform, not an assumed H=T+U.

methods.title: Derive motion and cyclic conservation from a Hamiltonian
methods.principle: Canonical first-order equations
steps: Differentiate H with respect to every momentum and coordinate
Pair coordinate derivatives with positive H momentum derivatives and momentum derivatives with negative H coordinate derivatives
Identify constant momenta from absent coordinates
Combine equations if an acceleration equation is needed
Interpret the dynamics in the stated coordinate system
methods.boundary: Constructing H and integrating the resulting equations are additional tasks when requested.

methods.title: Relate simple-harmonic period, stiffness, amplitude, speed and acceleration
methods.principle: The linear oscillator has frequency squared equal to restoring stiffness divided by inertia
steps: Identify the equilibrium-centered coordinate, inertia and restoring stiffness; for an LC circuit use charge q, inertia L and stiffness 1/C;infer a linear or torsional stiffness from restoring force/displacement or restoring torque/angle when supplied
Use omega squared=stiffness/inertia and T=2*pi/omega=1/f as applicable
Use acceleration=-omega squared*displacement, maximum speed=omega*amplitude and speed squared=omega squared*(amplitude squared-displacement squared)
Insert graph or measured data and solve the requested unknowns or ratios
Check independent data, positivity, units and whether a stated interval is a full cycle
methods.boundary: This applies known oscillator relations. Constructing a new restoring law, integrating a distributed inertia, fitting raw measurements, matching phase, or following an impact adds a task. If the source explicitly demands an energy derivation, preserve it rather than substituting a memorized speed relation. Electrical LC oscillations use exactly the same algebra after q replaces displacement and current replaces velocity.

methods.title: Relate force, impulse and momentum change
methods.principle: Net external impulse is the change of total momentum
steps: Choose the material system, inertial frame and interval
Resolve the initial and final momenta componentwise
Integrate each force component in time, use signed graph area, or differentiate supplied momentum to obtain force
Equate impulse to final minus initial momentum
Divide by duration only to obtain a time-averaged force
Separate contact force from net force when gravity or another external force matters
methods.boundary: A short collision does not establish conservation unless other impulses are negligible. Reversal requires signed velocities, and a graph magnitude needs its force direction separately. For electromagnetic momentum transfer,include the actual induction or discharge-current force and all receiving bodies;retained final field momentum cannot be assumed zero.

methods.title: Distinguish inertial motion from acceleration of the reference frame
methods.principle: Unforced bodies have constant velocity in an inertial frame; internal experiments do not determine absolute uniform translation
steps: Specify the observer and candidate frame motion
Describe an unforced test body or an accelerometer in that frame
Separate a real interaction from an apparent force due to frame acceleration
Explain what acceleration or rotation can be detected locally
State the assumptions and any confounding tilt or gravitational field
methods.boundary: No internal measurement identifies an absolute constant velocity, including relativistic uniform motion. Quantitative rotating-frame trajectories require explicit inertial-force equations.

methods.title: Assemble axial inertia from point masses or known component shapes
methods.principle: Additive second perpendicular-distance mass moments
steps: Identify the exact axis and each component mass
Use m*r_perpendicular squared for point masses or the correct known shape inertia for each extended component
Bring component inertias to the common axis when necessary
Sum material contributions and subtract removed material with its actual mass
Check thin-body assumptions and scaling
methods.boundary: A requested integral derivation is a separate required task; replacing it by a table value does not meet that request. A component at the center of mass is not automatically a point mass.

methods.title: Prove inertia identities from mass moments
methods.principle: Linearity and positivity of the defining second-moment integrals
steps: Insert the integral definitions of the required tensor entries
Combine or split mass domains as specified
Cancel shared squared-coordinate terms or impose the planar constraint
Use nonnegative squared-coordinate integrals for any inequality
Identify the exact equality condition
methods.boundary: Includes the perpendicular-axis identity and principal-moment triangle inequality; proving an eigenvector or changing origin requires the corresponding additional steps.

methods.title: Derive axial angular momentum of a rigid rotation
methods.principle: Rigid-body velocity and angular-momentum sum
steps: Write each particle velocity from fixed-axis angular motion
Evaluate its angular-momentum component about the axis
Sum the mass times squared perpendicular distance
Factor the common angular velocity
Identify the axial moment of inertia

methods.title: Integrate a moment of inertia about a specified axis
methods.principle: Second perpendicular-distance mass moment
steps: Determine the distance to the rotation axis
Choose coordinates and a mass element
Express uniform or varying density from the supplied mass distribution
Integrate squared axis-distance over the full body
Check units and size scaling
methods.boundary: Disk, sphere and lamina shapes change integration bounds, not the defining procedure.

methods.title: Determine principal axes and equal moments by symmetry
methods.principle: Mass-distribution invariance and the tensor eigenvector definition
steps: Pair mass elements under the stated reflection or rotation
Show which off-diagonal second moments vanish and which diagonal moments coincide
Apply the tensor to each proposed axis
Conclude its principal moment
Describe any degenerate family of axes

methods.title: Construct the inertia tensor of a mass distribution
methods.principle: Mass-weighted second moments about a specified origin
steps: Specify the origin, axes and mass element
Use mass-distribution symmetry to identify zero or equal entries
Sum or integrate r-squared delta-ij minus r-i r-j
Normalize the density with the total mass
Assemble the symmetric tensor
Check units and simple limiting shapes
methods.boundary: A single-axis moment is a restricted subset; a full tensor additionally requires products of inertia and their signs.

methods.title: Recover a central force from an orbit and area law
methods.principle: Conserved areal velocity and inverse Binet relation
steps: Use constant areal velocity to establish zero transverse acceleration
Write the supplied orbit as u(phi)
Differentiate it twice
Substitute into the radial acceleration identity
Express the resulting force in r
methods.boundary: This is inverse reconstruction of a force, not solving a known force law.

methods.title: Infer a Kepler conic from position, velocity or apsides
methods.principle: Energy and angular momentum determine conic scale and eccentricity
steps: Compute specific energy and angular momentum or infer conic scale from the supplied apsides
Determine eccentricity and semimajor axis
Fit the periapsis direction using position and the sign of radial velocity
Evaluate the requested radius or turning point
Classify bound and unbound branches
methods.boundary: Radius is measured from the force center, not altitude above its surface; tangent data remove the general radial-phase step.

methods.title: Apply the Kepler period and semimajor-axis relation
methods.principle: The square of a two-body inverse-square orbital period is proportional to the cube of the relative semimajor axis
steps: Identify the central or total mass appropriate to the two-body approximation
Use semimajor axis for an ellipse and center-based radius for a circle
Convert period and distance units consistently
Solve T squared=4*pi squared*a cubed/[G*(M+m)] or form a ratio with a reference orbit
For a specified orbital fraction use the corresponding time only when it is justified by symmetry
methods.boundary: This is application, not derivation from areal velocity. Comparable binary masses require the total mass and relative separation. Equal fractions of angle are not equal fractions of time in an eccentric orbit.

methods.title: Find an inverse-square orbital period from area and angular momentum
methods.principle: Constant areal velocity and ellipse geometry
steps: Compute ellipse area and areal velocity
Express angular momentum through the conic scale
Eliminate eccentricity to obtain the semimajor-axis law
Retain total mass for comparable-mass bodies
Apply the full-period or requested fractional-orbit time

methods.title: Differentiate a prescribed trajectory or velocity
methods.principle: Velocity and acceleration are successive time derivatives of position
steps: Differentiate the supplied position or velocity function
Evaluate the requested instants
Solve zero-velocity, zero-acceleration or crossing equations as required
Check all real roots against the physical time interval
Distinguish extrema of signed position from extrema or cusps of distance
methods.boundary: A fitted or prescribed polynomial is not necessarily a constant-acceleration trajectory.

methods.title: Read or construct motion graphs using slopes and areas
methods.principle: Position slope is velocity, velocity slope is acceleration and signed areas give accumulated changes
steps: Identify plotted axes, units and any reversed axis convention
Read tangents, secants, curvature or signed area as appropriate
Handle piecewise segments and changes of direction explicitly
Construct the related position, velocity or acceleration graph with consistent initial data
State the precision supported by a sketch or measured plot
methods.boundary: Coincidence in position does not imply equal slopes. Positive velocity is not the same as increasing velocity.

methods.title: Integrate a prescribed acceleration or velocity with initial data
methods.principle: Displacement and velocity change are time integrals
steps: Integrate the supplied time-dependent rate
Apply each initial condition at its actual specified time
Integrate a second time if position is required
Impose the requested crossing, rest or extremum condition
Check the solution and sign changes on the physical interval
methods.boundary: Use a signed velocity integral for displacement and split at turning times for distance. Do not silently set an integration constant to zero.

methods.title: Distinguish displacement, distance, velocity and acceleration
methods.principle: Average rates use endpoint changes while speed uses path length
steps: Choose the positive direction and the relevant time interval
Calculate signed displacement or velocity change from endpoints
Sum path lengths separately if average speed is requested
Divide by elapsed time
Check signs, units and the distinction between instantaneous and average quantities
methods.boundary: Equal endpoint positions do not imply zero instantaneous velocity. Equality of average speed and the magnitude of average velocity requires no reversal on the interval.

methods.title: Evaluate or compare nonrelativistic translational kinetic energies
methods.principle: Kinetic energy is one half mass times velocity-vector norm squared
steps: Choose the reference frame and obtain all velocity components
Form the squared speed, adding squared components without directional signs
Convert masses and speeds to consistent units
Evaluate or compare one half mass times speed squared
Invert for mass or speed and apply squared-speed scaling when requested
methods.boundary: Direction changes alone do not change this kinetic energy. A change of inertial frame can change it, unlike a mere relabeling or rotation of axes.

methods.title: Derive the generalized-coordinate kinetic-energy matrix
methods.principle: Cartesian velocity chain rule and a symmetric quadratic form
steps: Differentiate position vectors in time-independent coordinates
Substitute velocities into total kinetic energy
Collect coordinate-velocity products
Identify the mass-weighted dot-product matrix
Prove symmetry and positive kinetic energy on independent coordinates
methods.boundary: The purely quadratic expression requires time-independent coordinate transformations; moving constraints introduce linear and constant velocity terms.

methods.title: Derive charged-particle motion from a velocity-dependent electromagnetic Lagrangian
methods.principle: Minimal-coupling L=T+q v dot A-q Phi
steps: Express vector and scalar potentials in the chosen coordinates
Form the full velocity-dependent Lagrangian
Differentiate conjugate momenta and coordinate derivatives
Collect electric and magnetic terms
Interpret the resulting Lorentz equations
Analyze any additional trajectory constraint

methods.title: Derive constrained motion using Lagrange equations
methods.principle: Stationarity of action with independent generalized coordinates
steps: Choose independent coordinates and express the constraints
Express every position in those coordinates and time
Differentiate to obtain full inertial velocities including explicit time dependence
Construct translational and rotational kinetic energy and potential energy
Form L=T-U
Evaluate each Euler-Lagrange equation
Solve the coupled equations for the requested accelerations or interpret them
methods.boundary: Repeating a physical setup does not merge an explicitly requested Lagrange derivation with a Newton-force or energy-only derivation. Moving constraints generally do not conserve T+U.

methods.title: Find motion and constraint forces with Lagrange multipliers
methods.principle: Euler-Lagrange equations with holonomic constraint gradients
steps: Retain redundant coordinates and write the constraint equation
Introduce its multiplier into each Euler-Lagrange equation
Differentiate the constraint as needed to relate accelerations
Solve for accelerations and multiplier
Convert multiplier times constraint gradients into physical forces or torques
Check against Newton equations when requested
methods.boundary: The multiplier alone is not always a force: rescaling the constraint rescales the multiplier, while physical generalized forces remain invariant.

methods.title: Connect Cartesian Lagrange equations to Newton equations
methods.principle: Cartesian kinetic-energy derivatives and conservative force gradient
steps: Write the Cartesian kinetic energy and potential
Evaluate velocity and coordinate derivatives of L
Compare each Euler-Lagrange component with Newton second law
Add a nonconservative generalized force when specified
Extend over independent particle coordinates
methods.boundary: A nonconservative force is not silently represented by a position-only potential.

methods.title: Derive Hamiltonian partial-derivative identities
methods.principle: Chain rule for an invertible Legendre transformation
steps: Treat velocities as functions of coordinates, momenta and time
Differentiate sum p qdot minus L holding the specified independent variables fixed
Cancel velocity-derivative terms using p=L velocity derivative
Use Euler-Lagrange equations for coordinate derivatives
Obtain the requested q, p or explicit-time identity

methods.title: Compute and compare particle and total linear momentum
methods.principle: Vector momentum is mass times velocity
steps: Choose one inertial frame and axes
Resolve each velocity into signed components
Multiply by the corresponding mass and sum over the specified system
Recover magnitude and direction if requested
Keep the vector sum distinct from the sum of kinetic energies
methods.boundary: A system can have zero total momentum and nonzero kinetic energy. A finite collision requires a before/after conservation or impulse argument, not only this definition.

methods.title: Prove preservation of canonical phase-space volume
methods.principle: Hamiltonian phase-flow divergence vanishes
steps: Write the 2N phase-velocity components from Hamilton equations
Differentiate each with respect to its corresponding phase coordinate
Cancel mixed second derivatives in coordinate-momentum pairs
Apply the divergence theorem to a material phase volume
Conclude fine-grained volume and advected ensemble density are preserved
methods.boundary: Requires smooth canonical Hamiltonian flow; explicit time dependence does not invalidate the mixed-partial cancellation.

methods.title: Solve motion in crossed uniform electric and magnetic fields
methods.principle: Drift shift of transverse velocity
steps: Resolve the Lorentz-force components and identify invariant longitudinal motion
Set transverse acceleration to zero to determine the drift velocity
Subtract that drift from the velocity
Solve the remaining magnetic gyration
Integrate drift plus gyration and apply initial conditions
Classify trajectories for the requested initial speeds
methods.boundary: The same transverse equations arise for any constant force perpendicular to uniform B: replace qE by that force, including mg. A complete initial-value trajectory is distinct from a zero-deflection velocity-selector balance.

methods.title: Integrate nonrelativistic motion in a uniform magnetic field with optional parallel electric field
methods.principle: Decoupled longitudinal acceleration and transverse Newton-Lorentz rotation
steps: Resolve velocity parallel and perpendicular to the common field axis
Solve the coupled transverse velocity equations as a rotation
Integrate constant longitudinal acceleration,including zero electric field as the drift case
Integrate transverse positions and apply all initial conditions
Identify the guiding center,gyrofrequency and any changing pitch
methods.boundary: This is the full nonrelativistic trajectory route. Merely obtaining a known orbit radius is listed under circular-force balance. Relativistic parallel electric acceleration changes gamma and needs its own treatment.

methods.title: Find classical oscillator frequency splitting in a magnetic field
methods.principle: Restoring plus Lorentz force
steps: Write the transverse circular-mode force balance
Solve the resulting quadratic frequency equation
Expand in weak field when specified
Identify unchanged longitudinal motion and polarization

methods.title: Solve an isolated separation or collision from momentum conservation
methods.principle: Equal total momentum across a short event
steps: Choose one inertial frame and the isolated system
Express all before and after velocities in that frame including supplied relative velocities
Write componentwise momentum conservation
Apply the stated mass and velocity constraints
Solve for the unknown velocities
Repeat across successive isolated events when specified
methods.boundary: Kinetic energy is not assumed conserved unless the collision is explicitly elastic.

methods.title: Calculate force from a stream of intercepted mass
methods.principle: Momentum transferred per unit time
steps: Compute the swept or crossing volume per time
Multiply by mass density for mass flow
Determine each parcel momentum change
Multiply mass flow by velocity change with the correct sign
Include an explicitly supplied transfer or geometry factor

methods.title: Find the quadratic restoring force of a multi-coordinate system
methods.principle: Second-order potential expansion and Hessian
steps: Express each constrained spring length or energy in the independent coordinates
Expand to quadratic order about equilibrium
Collect squared and mixed-coordinate terms
Differentiate to obtain the linear restoring force
Inspect eigenvalues or diagonal curvatures for stability and isotropy
methods.boundary: A zero quadratic curvature needs higher-order analysis; isotropy does not by itself imply a positive restoring stiffness.

methods.title: Relate equilibrium and stability to potential energy in natural coordinates
methods.principle: Positive coordinate-dependent inertia and potential-energy curvature
steps: Write kinetic energy as one-half A(q) q-dot squared
Derive the full equation including the inertia-derivative term
Set velocity and acceleration to zero to identify stationary potential points
Use positive inertia and local energy or linearization to assess minima and maxima
Check whether explicit time dependence invalidates the premises
methods.boundary: A vanishing second derivative requires higher-order analysis. An accelerating constraint is not covered by a time-independent natural Lagrangian.

methods.title: Derive motion by resolving Newton equations in a moving basis
methods.principle: Time derivatives of position and local basis vectors
steps: Choose independent curvilinear coordinates
Differentiate position including basis-vector derivatives
Resolve the physical force into the same basis
Equate all acceleration components to force over mass
Impose initial data and test proposed constant-coordinate solutions
Use conservation laws only when their symmetry assumptions hold
methods.boundary: A proposed circular trajectory is not an externally imposed rigid constraint. Do not discard its normal equation.

methods.title: Derive total angular-momentum conservation from rotation symmetry
methods.principle: Invariance under a common infinitesimal azimuth shift
steps: Apply a common rotation to all particle coordinates
Set the infinitesimal Lagrangian change to zero
Sum the coordinate derivatives
Use Euler-Lagrange equations to convert to a time derivative
Identify the summed conjugate momentum as total angular momentum

methods.title: Resolve real and inertial forces in an accelerating or rotating frame
methods.principle: Newton second law with translation, centrifugal, Coriolis and Euler terms
steps: Specify the frame acceleration and angular velocity
Express position and frame-relative velocity in consistent axes
Add the applicable inertial force terms to the real forces
Project along free or constrained directions
Solve the requested force balance or equations
Check directions with cross products
methods.boundary: The Coriolis velocity is measured relative to the rotating frame; forces normal to a constraint may be reactions rather than acceleration in an allowed coordinate.

methods.title: Compute a trajectory from coupled equations of motion
methods.principle: Numerical initial-value integration
steps: Write a first-order position-velocity system from the force model
Supply all initial conditions and physical parameters
Integrate with controlled numerical tolerances
Detect the requested crossing or event
Plot or compare trajectories on consistent axes
Test a known limiting model and numerical convergence
methods.boundary: Spatially varying drag changes the force evaluation but not this integration procedure.

methods.title: Compute tangential impulses between circular and transfer orbits
methods.principle: Instantaneous velocity changes plus Kepler energy and angular momentum
steps: Set the transfer ellipse apsides from the two circular radii
Determine transfer speed at each apsis
Compare with the local circular speed to obtain each impulse or speed factor
Preserve the continuous radius and changed orbital constants across each impulse
Include speed change along the transfer when comparing initial and final circular speeds
methods.boundary: Inward transfers reverse perigee/apogee roles; the product of impulse factors alone is not the total speed ratio.

methods.title: Prove total momentum conservation or its pair-force converse
methods.principle: Newton pair-force balance and the derivative of total momentum
steps: Write the derivative of total momentum as the sum of particle forces
Separate external forces from ordered internal pairs
Group each internal pair once
Use equal and opposite forces to cancel it, or infer that pair condition for an isolated two-particle system
State the isolation and inertial-frame assumptions
methods.boundary: Angular momentum additionally requires vanishing internal torque, not only opposite forces.

methods.title: Construct many-particle potential energy from distinct pairs
methods.principle: Sum unordered pair energies once, excluding divergent point self energies
steps: List each unordered interacting pair once and any external potential contributions
Write the signed interaction energy with each actual pair separation
Sum all pairs for the assembly energy or only changed pairs for an energy difference
If forces are requested, differentiate only terms involving the selected particle with the correct relative-coordinate sign
Check action-reaction for internal forces and the chosen energy reference
methods.boundary: Adding a test charge changes only its interactions with the existing system; it does not repeat the energy already spent assembling the fixed sources. Derivation of a force is required only if requested.

methods.title: Shift a known inertia to a parallel displaced axis
methods.principle: Parallel-axis relation referenced to the center of mass
steps: Identify a known inertia for an axis through the center of mass
Determine the perpendicular offset to the requested parallel axis
Add M*d squared for the scalar moment, or M*(d squared identity-d outer d) for a requested tensor
When starting from a noncentral known axis, first subtract its central-axis correction
Check axis parallelism and nonnegative central inertia
methods.boundary: Do not apply I2=I1+M*d12 squared between two arbitrary noncentral axes. Full tensor requests also require off-diagonal terms and are not exhausted by a single scalar result.

methods.title: Derive the tensor parallel-axis relation
methods.principle: Translate second moments from the center of mass
steps: Write each position as its center-relative vector plus the displacement
Expand the tensor integrand
Cancel all first moments using the center definition
Collect the mass-weighted displacement tensor
Verify diagonal and off-diagonal signs

methods.title: Relate the period of a simple or physical pendulum to its geometry
methods.principle: For small angular motion, omega squared=m*g*d/I about the pivot
steps: Locate the center of gravity and its distance from the pivot
Use the pivot moment of inertia, retaining the extended-body contribution when present
For a simple pendulum set I=m*L squared and d=L
Apply T=2*pi*sqrt(I/[m*g*d]) and solve the requested period, geometry, gravity or inertia
Check the small-angle approximation and distinguish a full period from a half swing
methods.boundary: Replacing an extended body by a point at its center can change its period. Computing a composite inertia or a new restoring torque is an added step. In free fall there is no gravity-restored pendulum oscillation in the local uniform-field idealization.

methods.title: Solve a periodically driven linear oscillator by Fourier harmonics
methods.principle: Linearity and the frequency response of each harmonic
steps: Obtain the Fourier coefficients of the periodic force
Apply the complex oscillator response at each harmonic frequency
Include the static zero-frequency displacement
Sum the harmonic responses with their phases
Evaluate or plot the requested partial sums and compare resonance contributions
methods.boundary: This gives the long-time particular response; arbitrary transient initial conditions require an additional homogeneous solution.

methods.title: Evaluate a perturbed trajectory at its corrected impact time
methods.principle: First-order endpoint expansion
steps: Identify the unperturbed impact root
Expand the height equation around that root
Solve the first-order flight-time correction
Expand horizontal coordinates at the corrected time
Retain all terms of the requested order
Compare with the intended target
methods.boundary: The time correction may be negligible for a transverse displacement already first order but essential for an along-range displacement with a nonzero zeroth-order velocity.

methods.title: Describe one-dimensional phase portraits from energy contours
methods.principle: Autonomous Hamiltonian is constant along a trajectory
steps: Construct or use H(q,p)
Set it equal to the chosen energy
Find allowed coordinates and momentum branches
Identify turning points, equilibria and separatrices
Use Hamilton equations for direction of motion
Interpret closed and open contours

methods.title: Infer beam-spread constraints from conserved phase volume
methods.principle: Liouville preservation and transverse phase-space geometry
steps: Write the initial occupied phase volume from the specified distributions
Separate unchanged longitudinal factors
Relate transverse spatial narrowing to momentum-space extent
Account for correlations before equating products of marginal extents
Interpret downstream spreading and the limits of ideal focusing
methods.boundary: Liouville preserves occupied phase volume, not arbitrary products of marginal widths; equality of simple radius products needs the stated factorized or idealized beam assumption.

methods.title: Solve a pair of planar linear equations with a complex coordinate
methods.principle: Combine x and y into x+i y
steps: Write the two coupled linear equations
Multiply one by i and add
Solve the complex characteristic equation
Include the time-times-exponential solution for a repeated root
Fit the complex initial position and velocity
Recover real coordinates and interpret rotations

methods.title: Infer particle acceleration or an unknown force from a free-body diagram
methods.principle: The vector sum of external forces on the selected particle equals mass times its acceleration
steps: Select the body and identify every external interaction acting on it
Draw and label the actual forces without adding mass times acceleration as another force
Choose convenient fixed axes and resolve components
Set each force sum equal to mass times that acceleration component
Use zero acceleration only in a direction where the motion or constraint warrants it
Solve for the requested force, mass or acceleration and check signs
For terminal motion insert the given velocity-dependent resistance and solve the zero net-force equation for the admissible speed
methods.boundary: A normal force or tension need not equal weight. Multi-body internal contact forces require separate subsystem balances; nonconstant-force trajectories require an additional integration task.

methods.title: Eliminate time and integrate one-dimensional motion through v dv/dx
methods.principle: Newton equation with acceleration written as v dv/dx
steps: Resolve the signed force on the current direction-of-motion branch
Replace acceleration by v dv/dx
Separate the variables using the specified position or velocity dependence
Integrate between the supplied positions and speeds
Select physical velocity branches and nonnegative speed squared
Match ascent,descent or stopping segments when the force sign changes
methods.boundary: An arbitrary nonseparable force F(x,v) is not covered by this separation. A time trajectory requires an additional dt=dx/v integral.

methods.title: Obtain travel time or an oscillation period from position-dependent speed
methods.principle: Elapsed time is the oriented integral of inverse velocity along the physical path
steps: Obtain the position-dependent speed from the supplied propagation law or the mechanical energy relation
Find the allowed path and turning points and choose the direction of travel
Integrate dt=dx/v or the equivalent path-coordinate expression over the requested segment
For a full oscillation sum the outgoing and returning branches or use a justified symmetry factor
Evaluate or approximate the definite integral,using dimensionless variables when amplitude dependence is requested
Check integrability at zero-speed endpoints and invert for position only when requested
methods.boundary: A finite-amplitude pendulum generally gives an elliptic integral;its small-angle period is not an exact substitute. Deriving an unknown medium speed or force-energy relation can be a separately requested task.

methods.title: Construct a conservative potential or potential difference by a work integral
methods.principle: Potential change is minus the conservative force integral; electric potential uses force per unit charge
steps: Choose the potential reference and whether the quantity is energy or energy per unit charge
Integrate minus the corresponding force or field along a permitted convenient path
Split the path at regional formula changes and match additive constants
Include remaining-coordinate functions when reconstructing a multivariable potential
Check the negative gradient where defined
Convert a potential difference to particle work with the signed charge or mass when requested
methods.boundary: Infinite line and plane sources require finite potential references. A path cannot pass through a point or line singularity without a limiting construction. A constant shift changes neither fields nor work.

methods.title: Find and classify equilibria from potential energy
methods.principle: Stationary energy and local shape
steps: Differentiate the potential within its physical domain
Solve for stationary configurations

Use the second derivative or higher-order sign behavior to distinguish minima, maxima and neutral points; for several allowed displacement directions test each direction or the constrained Hessian,not just one coordinate
Check boundaries and contact constraints
Compare parameter regimes or plot as requested
A supplied force or diagram permits the equivalent small-displacement restoring-force or restoring-torque test; state the allowed perturbations

methods.title: Relate work or energy transfer to average and instantaneous power
methods.principle: Power is the energy-transfer rate; force supplies F dot v and an axial torque supplies torque times angular speed
steps: Identify the energy transfer and its sign for the selected system
For a finite interval divide transferred work or energy by elapsed time, or integrate the supplied power history
For instantaneous power calculate force dot application-point velocity, or torque dot angular velocity for rigid rotation
Use mass-flow, event frequency, travel time or vertical-speed geometry when needed
Keep useful mechanical power separate from total metabolic or input power
Convert units and apply efficiency or capacity limits only when stated
For a finite energy reservoir solve available energy equals the integrated power,including any stated duty cycle
methods.boundary: Average force times average speed is not generally average power; constant power does not imply constant force. A fuel-endurance calculation uses an explicitly assumed relation between fuel use and mechanical power.

methods.title: Find the reachable boundary for fixed-speed launches
methods.principle: Envelope over launch angle
steps: Write the vacuum trajectory at arbitrary launch angle
Parameterize the angle by its tangent or another monotone variable
Impose a real launch solution or maximize height at fixed horizontal distance
Solve the limiting discriminant or derivative condition
Rotate the boundary about the symmetry axis if required

methods.title: Find equilibrium by completing a quadratic potential square
methods.principle: Shift of origin in a quadratic energy
steps: Combine the quadratic and linear potential terms
Complete the square
Identify the shifted equilibrium and unchanged curvature
Choose the specified energy zero
Interpret the translated coordinate
methods.boundary: The same algebra appears in the shifted quantum oscillator, which additionally requires eigenstate and eigenenergy interpretation.

methods.title: Transform classical velocities between moving observers
methods.principle: Relative velocity is the vector difference of velocities in a common reference frame
steps: Label each object and reference frame explicitly
Write the vector addition or subtraction relation
Resolve components and impose the desired ground direction or heading
Recover magnitudes, directions and travel times using the appropriate frame
Check reachability and distinguish shortest crossing time from landing directly opposite
methods.boundary: Use Galilean addition for the nonrelativistic context. Equal paddling effort is interpreted as equal speed relative to still water in the ideal model; wind direction is where air moves, not where it comes from.

methods.title: Find a narrow resonance width from its response function
methods.principle: Half-maximum condition near the peak
steps: Write the squared response and identify the varied frequency
Determine the peak value to the justified order
Expand the slowly varying factors near resonance while retaining detuning
Solve the two half-maximum equations
Subtract their frequencies and state the narrow-resonance approximation

methods.title: Balance forces and torques for a rigid body or linked rigid bodies
methods.principle: Zero net force and zero net torque in static or uniform-translation equilibrium
steps: Draw the external forces at their actual application points for each required body
Locate each center of gravity and resolve force components and perpendicular lever arms
Choose a torque origin that removes unknown reactions, or use the origin explicitly requested
Solve the independent force and torque balance equations
For linked bodies isolate components and use opposite internal interaction forces
At tipping or detachment set the appropriate one-sided support reaction to zero and check physical signs
methods.boundary: A purely particle force balance has no independent moment equation. Friction thresholds, elastic deformation, a requested regression or subsequent dynamics add required tasks. Multi-support problems can be underdetermined without deformation or a specified force-sharing assumption.

methods.title: Find rigid-body motion across an impact or off-center impulse
methods.principle: Linear and angular impulse-momentum balances with the actual contact constraints
steps: Choose the body or colliding system and a fixed inertial or center-of-mass torque origin
Include all external impulses,including any pivot or support impulse
Relate the summed linear impulse to center-of-mass momentum change
Relate the moments of impulses to angular-momentum change;choose an origin that eliminates an unknown contact impulse when useful
Apply the specified contact or pivot velocity constraint and solve for translation,rotation and requested reaction impulses
Add center velocity and angular velocity cross displacement at other points
If an elastic impact requires energy conservation,couple the separately listed translational-plus-rotational energy balance
methods.boundary: Momentum need not be conserved for a pivoted body because the pivot supplies an impulse. Angular momentum about the impact point can nevertheless be conserved when its net external angular impulse vanishes. Do not omit support impulses or assume all rigid impacts are elastic.

methods.title: Calculate rigid-body kinetic energy from translation and rotation
methods.principle: Center-of-mass decomposition or instantaneous rest point
steps: Specify the center velocity and angular velocity
Choose the corresponding inertia about the center or a point instantaneously at rest
Add center translational and center rotational energies or use rotation about the rest point alone
Apply no-slip relations where present
Compare equivalent expressions without double-counting translation

methods.title: Balance momentum with mass entering or leaving a body
methods.principle: Material-system momentum conservation with an explicit mass flux
steps: Choose an inertial frame and identify the body and transferred parcel
Express incoming or outgoing parcel velocity in that frame
Expand the body-plus-parcel momentum over a small interval
Include external impulse and retain first-order mass-transfer terms
Obtain the variable-mass equation with the correct sign
Use the supplied flux or mass history and check limiting cases
methods.boundary: For accretion, d(Mv)/dt=F_external only when incoming material is at rest in the chosen frame. For exhaust, use its velocity relative to the rocket rather than dropping the flux term.

methods.title: Find fuel expenditure for a hovering rocket
methods.principle: Thrust-weight balance with changing mass
steps: Set mass-loss rate times exhaust speed equal to instantaneous weight
Separate the resulting mass-time equation
Integrate between initial and allowed final mass
Solve for hover duration
Check that the allowed burned fraction is between zero and one

methods.title: Integrate a rocket burn with fixed exhaust speed
methods.principle: Rocket equation and known mass history
steps: Write the thrust term and specified external acceleration
Substitute the mass history or change independent variable to mass
Integrate the velocity equation with the initial condition
Update the mass at stage jettisons before integrating subsequent burns
Integrate velocity if height is requested
Check liftoff and fuel-exhaustion bounds
methods.boundary: A hover condition or velocity-dependent external force introduces a different relation to solve.

methods.title: Solve a constant-burn rocket with linear resistance
methods.principle: Separable velocity-mass equation
steps: Insert constant mass-loss rate and linear drag into rocket momentum balance
Replace time by the remaining mass
Separate the velocity and mass factors
Integrate with the initial velocity
Solve for velocity and check the zero-drag limit

methods.title: Derive a point trajectory on a rolling circle
methods.principle: No-slip translation plus rotation
steps: Relate center translation to the rotation angle by no slip
Add the rotating radius vector to the center position
Project onto the specified axes
Fit endpoint or initial-position constants
Eliminate or retain the angular parameter as required

methods.title: Solve constrained translation and rotation from force and torque
methods.principle: Newton equations for the center of mass and rotation about it
steps: Draw all external forces and identify their application points
Write the center-of-mass force equation and the torque equation with the correct central inertia
Derive the rolling or unwinding constraint from the actual contact or string motion
Eliminate reaction or tension forces to determine acceleration and angular acceleration
Check contact and available static friction where relevant
