methods.title: Explain the conventional phonon interaction link between resistance and pairing
methods.principle: Electron-phonon scattering and effective attraction
steps: Identify how lattice scattering degrades normal-state current
Identify the attractive pairing channel produced by the same coupling in the stated model
Compare the qualitative coupling-strength effects
State that the trend is model-dependent rather than a universal material law

methods.title: Compare material stress or strain with a yield or failure limit
methods.principle: Stress is internal force per load-bearing area
steps: Identify the relevant load-bearing area and normal or shear force
Calculate stress and compare with the stated elastic or breaking limit
Apply any explicit safety fraction or allowable strain
Solve for maximum load, minimum section or admissible motion
Distinguish reversible elastic response, permanent deformation and fracture
methods.boundary: Young modulus measures stiffness, not failure strength. Idealized textbook limits do not establish safe limits for real structures or bodies.

methods.title: Assess accessible states and finite-time sampling
methods.principle: An allowed state count is not the number of states actually visited
steps: Count allowed states under the physical constraints
Estimate at most rate times elapsed time sampling events
Compare orders of magnitude using logarithms
Distinguish accessibility from exhaustive visitation
Explain probabilistic equilibration and practical irreversibility
methods.boundary: Repeated correlated visits make rate-times-time an upper bound on distinct states, not proof that each visit is new.

methods.title: Calculate the leading thermal displacement from weak anharmonicity
methods.principle: Perturbative Boltzmann averages about a stable quadratic minimum
steps: Locate the potential minimum and expand through the first asymmetric term
Keep the quadratic term in the Boltzmann exponential
Expand the anharmonic exponential to controlled order
Evaluate numerator and denominator with Gaussian moments
Extract the first nonzero mean displacement and thermal expansion
Compare with the specified material estimate and state confinement limits
methods.boundary: A bare cubic polynomial is not a globally stable potential. The expansion is local within a stable well, not an exact integral of an unbounded cubic potential.

methods.title: Estimate a peak width from total weight divided by peak height
methods.principle: A rectangular peak with the same area and height
steps: Obtain the total multiplicity summed over allocations
Obtain the maximum single-allocation multiplicity
Retain prefactors when dividing them
Interpret their ratio as an effective width in allocation units
Divide by the full allowed range for a relative-width estimate
methods.boundary: This area-height estimate is a separately requested route, not a quadratic Taylor expansion.

methods.title: Find level population ratios or infer temperature
methods.principle: Canonical state probabilities are proportional to Boltzmann weights
steps: Identify the energy difference and level degeneracies
Distinguish one microstate from an entire energy level
Form the degeneracy-weighted exponential population ratio
Normalize if the specified state list is complete
Invert for temperature or evaluate the requested ratio
Check whether particle exchange or an omitted continuum invalidates the fixed-state model
methods.boundary: A ratio of two bound-level probabilities does not require a full partition sum. Ionization creates translational states and changes particle number, so it is not just one extra fixed atomic level.

methods.title: Determine Bose condensation and condensate thermodynamics
methods.principle: Excited-state saturation leaves excess particles in the ground state
steps: Construct the density of states for the specified box or trap
Separate the ground occupation from the excited continuum
Test infrared convergence at chemical potential equal to the ground energy
Solve excited-state saturation for the condensation temperature
Obtain condensate fraction, energy and heat capacity below the transition
Check finite-size and interaction limitations
methods.boundary: Absence of condensation in the ideal homogeneous two-dimensional thermodynamic limit does not mean a finite box cannot have appreciable ground-state occupation. Trap density of states changes the condensation exponent.

methods.title: Compute an equilibrium average from Boltzmann weights
methods.principle: Normalized canonical probability measure
steps: Specify the energy and state-space measure
Form the Boltzmann weight
Evaluate the partition normalization
Integrate or sum the observable times the weight
Divide by normalization or differentiate log partition function
Examine low- and high-parameter limits
methods.boundary: For orientations the solid-angle measure includes sine theta. A single-particle independent model omits correlations and local-field corrections.

methods.title: Derive a classical partition function by phase-space integration
methods.principle: Boltzmann weights integrated with the correct state-counting measure
steps: Specify the allowed coordinate and momentum domains
Include the appropriate phase-space cell factor
Factor independent coordinates when permitted
Rescale variables to evaluate convergent integrals
Differentiate log Z for averages
Check dimensions and the continuum approximation
methods.boundary: Classical continuum integration requires many accessible quantum states. A potential tending to a constant at infinity does not confine a canonical particle on an infinite line.

methods.title: Count discrete arrangements and their probabilities
methods.principle: Product rule, permutations and combinations with the stated distinguishability
steps: Specify what makes two microstates distinct
Enumerate small cases or construct a one-to-one counting representation
Divide out ordering only when it is physically unobserved
Count the allowed and requested arrangements
Normalize by the total equally likely microstate count
Tabulate or plot the requested macrostate probabilities
methods.boundary: Coins, paramagnetic up/down choices and fixed-card subsets share combination counting. Unrestricted quanta in distinguishable oscillators first need the stars-and-bars representation; record that setup explicitly.

methods.title: Find an exchange distribution for two weakly coupled systems
methods.principle: Multiply independent multiplicities at fixed subsystem macrostate and sum allowed allocations
steps: Choose the exchange variable and its allowed range
Express the other subsystem variable from the conserved total
Compute each subsystem multiplicity
Multiply for each allocation
Sum to normalize probabilities
Identify most and least probable allocations and interpret fluctuations
methods.boundary: The individual multiplicity law can be binomial or oscillator stars-and-bars. Equal subsystem sizes do not imply that all allocations are equally likely.

methods.title: Find an expected event count by conditioning on the next state
methods.principle: Law of total expectation with an absorbing endpoint
steps: List the allowed downward or absorbing transitions and their conditional probabilities
Set the terminal state expected remaining count to zero
Write each other expectation as one event plus the probability-weighted remaining expectations
Solve the recurrence from lower to higher states or the corresponding finite linear system
Multiply by the initial ensemble size when requested and distinguish the expected count from a certain realized count
methods.boundary: Counting distinct possible photon energies is not counting emitted photons. Even when every atom reaches its ground state,the total photon count fluctuates across cascades.

methods.title: Normalize a continuous density and integrate probabilities and moments
methods.principle: Probability is the integral of a nonnegative density
steps: Identify support and density (take the modulus squared first when an amplitude is supplied).
Normalize, or check an already normalized density.

Integrate over the requested interval or against the requested observable,including inverse powers when convergent;use cumulative differences or a justified small-bin density-times-width approximation when appropriate
Obtain mode, spread and limiting cases or sketch from the same density when requested.
When a probability is specified,invert its cumulative relation for the requested parameter;preserve its support and monotonic branch
methods.boundary: Does not include deriving a density from dynamics or applying a momentum differential operator. A Maxwell tail fraction alone is not an escape rate:collisions,replenishment and the finite number of particles matter. Spatial density and radial density have different volume measures.

methods.title: Transform a continuous density,including uniform-time samples
methods.principle: Preserve probability or spectral weight with the absolute Jacobian and all inverse branches
steps: Identify the original density,its measure and support;uniform-time sampling has density one over the full sampling interval
Write the map to the requested variable and partition it into invertible branches
Use the absolute Jacobian on every branch;for a motion sample it is inverse speed or inverse rate
Sum branch contributions or integrate over unobserved angular coordinates with the proper volume factor
Normalize or verify the conserved total weight on the transformed support
Integrate requested probabilities or moments and inspect endpoint singularities
methods.boundary: Use an absolute Jacobian,include both sides of a turning trajectory,and do not treat density at one point as a point probability. A normalized sampling density and an unnormalized spectral energy density preserve different total weights.

methods.title: Count continuum modes by a momentum-space shell
methods.principle: Quantum state cell and dispersion relation
steps: Choose boundary conditions and their momentum-cell volume
Count the appropriate shell fraction and polarization or spin multiplicity
Divide shell volume by cell volume
Change variables from momentum to frequency or energy with its Jacobian
Specify whether the result is total or per real-space volume
methods.boundary: Use standing-wave octants or full traveling-wave space consistently; positive frequency does not mean negative momentum is physically forbidden.

methods.title: Discrete probabilities, means and spread
methods.principle: Normalized frequency weights
steps: Tabulate outcome multiplicities and divide by total count.
Sum weighted first and second moments; compute variance and standard deviation.
Locate mode and cumulative median if requested; compare the two variance formulas.
methods.boundary: Discrete weighted sums, not continuous integrals or sampling simulations.

methods.title: Compute thermodynamic curves from discrete microstate counts
methods.principle: Centered finite differences of energy and entropy
steps: Enumerate the allowed energy/occupation rows
Compute exact or log multiplicities and entropy
Estimate temperature with centered energy-to-entropy differences
Estimate heat capacity from neighboring energy and temperature values
Preserve unavailable endpoints and singular temperatures
Plot the requested thermodynamic curves and explain finite-size artifacts
methods.boundary: Do not replace requested finite-system numerical derivatives with a smooth thermodynamic-limit curve or differentiate across an infinite-temperature discontinuity blindly.

methods.title: Calculate entropy from specified accessible microstates
methods.principle: S=k log multiplicity
steps: Identify the constraints and observation time scale defining accessible states
Construct or use the appropriate multiplicity
Multiply independent counts or sum fluctuating allocations before taking the logarithm
Evaluate entropy or its difference
Compare extensive and subextensive contributions and state the role of distinguishability
methods.boundary: Log of a sum is not the sum of logs. A single fixed allocation and all accessible allocations have different multiplicities.

methods.title: Estimate entropy from the number of active particles
methods.principle: For the stated ordinary thermal regime entropy is of order Nk
steps: Estimate composition and mass per thermal particle
Convert total mass to particle number
Include additional independently active species such as ionized electrons
Multiply by k with an explicit order-one or logarithmic uncertainty
Compare systems without claiming an exact state-function value
methods.boundary: This heuristic is not valid for arbitrary ordered low-temperature systems; a black-hole estimate also needs a separate bound on particle energy.

methods.title: Apply exponential decay or relaxation toward a constant limiting value
methods.principle: A constant fractional decay rate for the displacement from equilibrium
steps: Identify the initial value, final value and elapsed time
Write x(t)=x_final+(x_initial-x_final)*exp(-t/tau)
Determine tau from the specified rate, half-life or physical time constant
Evaluate the requested value or invert the exponential for time or rate
For consecutive stages carry the actual ending value into the next stage
For quantities proportional to x squared, square the exponential factor
methods.boundary: Applying a known exponential law is distinct from deriving a differential equation and integrating it. Radioactive lifetimes require the correct reference frame. Circuit relaxation requires the actual Thevenin resistance and final voltage, which need not be zero; energy decays twice as fast as charge for fixed capacitance.

methods.title: Calculate spin polarization of a degenerate Fermi gas
methods.principle: Zeeman-shifted spin densities respond at the Fermi surface
steps: Separate the spin-resolved density of states and Zeeman energy shifts
Enforce a common chemical potential and total particle number
Integrate occupied up and down populations
Form magnetic moment times their difference
Expand in weak field if specified
Include fixed-number Sommerfeld corrections for the requested low-temperature response
methods.boundary: Do not use the independent localized-spin Curie law for a filled Fermi sea. The weak-field result assumes the Zeeman energy is small compared with the relevant Fermi scale.

methods.title: Estimate a spatial coherence scale from a thin thermal Fermi shell
methods.principle: Linearized dispersion at the Fermi surface
steps: Relate a small excitation-energy width to vF times momentum width
Set that energy width by the stated temperature scale
Apply the uncertainty relation to the momentum width
Estimate the spatial extent
methods.boundary: Use a change in p-squared about nonzero pF, not the energy of an isolated zero-momentum particle.

methods.title: Derive zero-temperature Fermi-gas scales and thermodynamics
methods.principle: Fill every available single-particle state up to the Fermi surface
steps: Construct the density of states with the actual dimension, dispersion and degeneracy
Integrate it to the fixed particle number to find the Fermi energy
Integrate energy times the density of states for total energy
Differentiate at fixed particle number for pressure or compressibility
Evaluate the Fermi temperature and compare thermal or relativistic scales
State whether the nonrelativistic or ultrarelativistic approximation applies
methods.boundary: Nuclear spin-isospin degeneracy, electron spin, spatial dimension and dispersion change state counting. A gas at temperature comparable to the Fermi temperature is neither deeply degenerate nor safely classical.

methods.title: Solve a finite trapped Bose gas using discrete levels
methods.principle: Discrete Bose occupations must sum to the finite prescribed particle number
steps: Enumerate energy levels with their exact degeneracies
Choose an energy zero and keep chemical potential strictly below the ground state
Sum Bose occupations with a convergence-tested cutoff
Solve the finite-number constraint at each temperature
Distinguish occupation of one state from all states in a degenerate energy level
Compare finite-system crossover with continuum condensation estimates
methods.boundary: This discrete mean-occupation calculation uses the grand-canonical number constraint; it is not an exact canonical fixed-number fluctuation calculation.

methods.title: Obtain thermodynamic functions from a canonical partition function
methods.principle: F=-kT log Z and its natural-variable derivatives
steps: Construct the full-system partition function with the correct particle statistics or subsystem product
Take its logarithm and use Stirling only in the stated regime
Obtain F and differentiate at fixed natural variables for entropy, pressure and chemical potential
Include implicit temperature dependence of internal factors
Form other potentials or check Euler relations
Preserve the energy reference and low-temperature limitations
methods.boundary: For dilute indistinguishable particles Z=z to N divided by N factorial; localized independent oscillators are distinguishable subsystems and do not get this factorial.

methods.title: Count ideal-gas microstates from phase-space volume
methods.principle: One independent state per h to the dimension and indistinguishable-particle correction
steps: Determine the number of positional and momentum coordinates
Write the fixed-total-energy momentum hypersphere
Combine positional volume with the momentum shell or enclosed volume
Divide by h to the total dimension and by N factorial where appropriate
Use the stated large-system approximation
Track the energy-window convention before dropping subextensive factors
methods.boundary: In two spatial dimensions there are 2N momentum coordinates, not N. Counting a shell and counting all states below energy agree only at the stated thermodynamic accuracy.

methods.title: Estimate equilibrium fluctuations from a multiplicity peak
methods.principle: Quadratic expansion of log multiplicity about its maximum
steps: Find the maximizing allocation under the conserved total
Expand its logarithm through the quadratic deviation term
Exponentiate to a Gaussian with the retained peak normalization
Identify variance or the explicitly requested width convention
Compare deviations with the resulting scale
State the near-peak and large-system regime
methods.boundary: Standard deviation, full width at half maximum and full one-over-e width differ by factors; do not interchange their names.

methods.title: Evaluate or verify entropy from a probability distribution
methods.principle: Entropy is minus k times the probability-weighted log probability
steps: List normalized microstate probabilities
Sum minus k p log p using zero log zero equal to zero
Insert uniform probabilities for a microcanonical ensemble
Insert canonical probabilities and identify mean energy plus k log Z
Compare with the thermodynamic entropy expression
methods.boundary: An energy-level probability must include its degeneracy correctly; treating a degenerate level as one microstate loses internal entropy.

methods.title: Derive number moments and fluctuations from grand-partition derivatives
methods.principle: Differentiating grand weights with respect to chemical potential brings down particle number
steps: Hold temperature, volume and the state energies fixed
Differentiate the grand partition sum with respect to chemical potential
Identify first and second number moments
Subtract the square of the mean
Express the variance as kT times the number susceptibility
Apply the equation of state for a specified gas
methods.boundary: This is a derivative proof, not merely evaluation of a supplied number-fluctuation formula.

methods.title: Derive thermodynamics from the grand partition function
methods.principle: The Gibbs entropy of grand weights gives Phi=U-TS-mu N=-kT log Xi
steps: Insert normalized grand probabilities into the Gibbs entropy
Identify mean energy and mean particle number
Rearrange to the grand potential
Differentiate with its natural variables for the requested observables
Use Phi=-PV only when homogeneity and extensivity justify it
methods.boundary: An energy differential equation alone admits an entropy-reference integration constant. A finite trapped system or a system with surface terms need not obey Phi=-PV in the homogeneous bulk sense.

methods.title: Calculate particle-exchange probabilities and binding occupancy
methods.principle: Grand-canonical weights include both energy and exchanged particle number
steps: Enumerate allowed subsystem states with energies, particle counts and degeneracies
Form exp[-beta(E-mu N)] for each microstate
Sum the grand partition function
Normalize and average the requested occupancy or state indicator
Relate reservoir chemical potential to its density or partial pressure
If the reservoir population is not fixed independently impose the full particle balance
methods.boundary: The probability of a two-particle occupied state is not the mean fraction of occupied sites. Cooperativity changes the double-occupancy energy, not simply a degeneracy factor.

methods.title: Determine which discrete excitations survive at low temperature
methods.principle: Boltzmann suppression compared with energy gaps
steps: Order the relevant levels and their degeneracies
Compare their gaps with kBT
Suppress inaccessible excitations and identify the surviving sector
Distinguish equilibrium populations from slow conversion or kinetic trapping

methods.title: Apply known Maxwell thermal speed scales and their temperature dependence
methods.principle: Boltzmann kinetic-energy weight times the velocity-space measure
steps: Identify particle mass,absolute temperature and whether a component,mean speed,most probable speed or rms speed is requested
Select its established Maxwell formula with the correct numerical factor and spatial dimension
Evaluate the speed or invert its square-root temperature-to-mass scaling
For a requested distribution plot use the supplied normalized Maxwell density with dimensioned axes
Explain which distribution changes when temperature,density or particle mass changes
methods.boundary: Deriving a speed density requires a Jacobian;deriving its moments or integrating tails is listed under continuous-density integration. Do not confuse a one-component thermal width with the three-dimensional rms speed.

methods.title: Derive temperature, energy and heat capacity from multiplicity or entropy
methods.principle: Inverse temperature is the fixed-constraint entropy derivative
steps: Take k times log multiplicity if entropy is not yet given
Express entropy in the actual energy variable
Differentiate at fixed particle number, geometry and specified external fields
Invert to energy as a function of temperature
Differentiate for the appropriate heat capacity
Check low- and high-energy or temperature limits
methods.boundary: This entropy-derivative route is not interchangeable with an explicitly requested partition-function derivation, though their resulting functions can agree.

methods.title: Compute a density of an incoherent ensemble
methods.principle: Classical mixing of quantum probability densities
steps: Specify ensemble probabilities explicitly
Form the weighted sum of member densities without amplitude cross terms
Normalize the weights
Integrate angular variables when a radial density is requested
methods.boundary: An energy eigenvalue alone does not fix weights within a degenerate subspace.

methods.title: Simulate a transformed distribution and compare a histogram
methods.principle: Uniform random sampling and change of variable
steps: Draw uniform random times across the stated period.
Transform times through the trajectory, form a density-normalized histogram.
Overlay the analytic density on the same support and compare finite-sample agreement.
methods.boundary: Computational sampling is an extra requested task, not an analytic density calculation.

methods.title: Calculate canonical properties from a truncated or numerical spectrum
methods.principle: Weighted finite sums approximate the specified partition sum
steps: Enumerate allowed levels and degeneracies without extending the model beyond its domain
Compute stable Boltzmann sums and energy moments over temperature
Obtain mean energy and heat capacity from derivatives or variance
Increase or decrease the cutoff to test the relevant truncation
Plot the requested normalized curves
Compare with limiting models or data
methods.boundary: A physically truncated spectrum and a numerical approximation to an infinite spectrum have different high-temperature limits; do not mistake artificial saturation for the original infinite model.

methods.title: Count quantum configurations at fixed particle number and excitation
methods.principle: Indistinguishability and occupancy restrictions determine the allowed configurations
steps: List single-particle levels and their allowed occupancies
Enforce the total particle number and total energy simultaneously
Count bosonic, fermionic or distinguishable configurations without double counting
Average level occupation over equal-weight fixed-energy states
Map equally spaced excitations to integer partitions when justified
Retain finite-particle restrictions when using partition asymptotics
methods.boundary: For equally spaced levels, unrestricted partitions apply to excitation quanta smaller than the number of particles. Distinguishable labeled configurations use different combinatorial weights.

methods.title: Infer an oscillator energy spacing from a heat-capacity curve
methods.principle: Einstein heat capacity is a universal function of kT/epsilon
steps: Subtract nonvibrational contributions when needed
Normalize by the number of oscillators times k
Match one or several source-curve points to the dimensionless Einstein function
Infer epsilon from the horizontal temperature scale
Compare curve shape and explain low-temperature model discrepancies
methods.boundary: A crystal has three oscillators per atom; one diatomic vibrational mode has one oscillator per molecule. A fitted Einstein energy is not proof that the real low-temperature solid obeys the Einstein model.

methods.title: Quantum oscillator partition function and heat capacity
methods.principle: Canonical weights and equally spaced levels
steps: Sum the Boltzmann weights as a geometric series including the ground-state offset
Differentiate log Z to obtain mean energy
Differentiate with temperature and multiply by the oscillator count for heat capacity
Check temperature limits and sketch the comparison with the classical result

methods.title: Test convergence and physical truncation of a partition sum
methods.principle: Convergence of the degeneracy-weighted Boltzmann series
steps: Write the large-level behavior of energy and degeneracy
Determine whether individual terms vanish and whether the sum converges
Identify the physical assumption that fails for the arbitrarily extended states
State the environment,volume or cutoff needed for a meaningful model
methods.boundary: Low-temperature suppression of a finite number of levels does not cure an infinite divergent series.

methods.title: Solve quantum-gas number conservation for chemical potential
methods.principle: The integrated occupation must equal the fixed particle number
steps: Build the density-of-states-weighted Fermi or Bose number integral
Scale energy and temperature to dimensionless variables
Bracket chemical potential in its physically allowed domain
Evaluate and solve the number constraint with controlled quadrature or an available analytic integral
Use the solved chemical potential in energy and response integrals
Test convergence and classical or degenerate limits
methods.boundary: A Bose continuum number integral ceases to represent the macroscopically occupied ground state below condensation. Separate that state before applying this procedure there.

methods.title: Evaluate quantum state occupations and their classical limits
methods.principle: A single-state grand sum yields Bose or Fermi mean occupation
steps: Specify allowed particle counts in one single-particle state
Derive the normalized grand weights when requested,or use the established Bose/Fermi mean-occupation law for a direct evaluation
Compute its mean or individual occupation probabilities as requested
Account separately for energy-level degeneracy
Compare with the classical small-fugacity limit or particle-hole symmetry
State the actual error criterion for a numerical approximation
For Planck oscillator quanta set chemical potential to zero and multiply mean occupation by the energy quantum;add a zero-point offset only when the stated energy convention includes it
methods.boundary: A mean occupation is not a probability for a particular particle number. A hypothetical occupancy cap of two is a distinct grand sum, not ordinary fermion or boson statistics.

methods.title: Derive the leading quantum-statistical correction to a dilute gas
methods.principle: A small-fugacity expansion modifies the classical equation of state
steps: Expand Bose or Fermi occupation in powers of fugacity
Integrate the density of states for number and grand potential
Invert the number-density series to the required order
Substitute into pressure using the justified bulk grand-potential relation
Convert the coefficient to the specified particle or molar virial convention
Include spin degeneracy and distinguish statistical corrections from interactions
methods.boundary: The leading boson pressure correction is negative and fermion correction positive; their magnitudes also depend on mass and spin degeneracy, not only statistics.

methods.title: Relate independent random steps to displacement fluctuations
methods.principle: Independent zero-mean increments have additive variances
steps: Express net displacement as a sum of signed steps
Obtain its mean and most probable location
Add independent step variances to get rms displacement
Relate step count to elapsed time using the collision time
Compare with diffusion scaling and state dimensional/order-one assumptions
methods.boundary: A zero mean displacement does not imply zero typical distance from the starting point.

methods.title: Approximate a rigid-rotor partition sum in a controlled temperature regime
methods.principle: Rotational degeneracy and quadratic angular-momentum energy set the state sum
steps: List allowed j values and their 2j+1 weights
Include molecular symmetry and nuclear-spin restrictions where specified
At high temperature approximate the sum by an integral with the correct symmetry factor
At low temperature retain the ground manifold and first allowed excitation
Differentiate for energy and heat capacity
Check the range and compare with a converged sum
methods.boundary: An identical-nucleus symmetry factor of one half is a high-temperature simplification, not a replacement for even/odd restrictions at low temperature.

methods.title: Find carrier populations and chemical potential from band states and neutrality
methods.principle: Band occupation and donor occupation must satisfy charge neutrality
steps: Specify conduction and valence band edges and density-of-states prefactors
Integrate electron and hole occupations using justified dilute approximations
Include donor charge-state degeneracy when present
Impose electron-hole or donor charge balance
Solve chemical potential and carrier density over temperature
Check the dilute regime and onset of intrinsic carriers
methods.boundary: A midgap chemical potential requires matching electron and hole density-of-states prefactors. Inferring conductivity from carrier density also assumes a specified or slowly varying mobility.

methods.title: Calculate low-temperature corrections of a degenerate Fermi gas
methods.principle: Only a narrow shell near the chemical potential changes occupation
steps: Write particle-number and observable integrals with their density of states
Expand around the chemical potential using Fermi-window moments
Use parity to identify vanishing terms
First solve the fixed-number condition for the chemical-potential shift
Substitute that shift into the observable expansion
Differentiate only after preserving the appropriate constraints
methods.boundary: Holding chemical potential at its zero-temperature value can miss terms of the same order as the requested energy or response correction.

methods.title: Distinguish frozen spin-isomer fractions from thermal interconversion
methods.principle: A fixed-composition mixture averages component energies while an equilibrating mixture sums state weights
steps: Construct even- and odd-j rotational partition sums
Include the assigned nuclear-spin multiplicities
For frozen composition combine component heat capacities with fixed fractions
For catalyzed equilibrium form a single weighted partition sum before differentiating
Convert the dimensionless scale to the appropriate isotope temperature
Compare freeze-out and population-redistribution features
methods.boundary: A weighted average of component heat capacities is not the equilibrium heat capacity when their weights change with temperature. Deuterium also changes the moment of inertia and energy spacing.

methods.title: Approximate factorial multiplicities without losing relevant prefactors
methods.principle: Stirling expansion of factorials or log factorials
steps: Write the exact factorial ratio first
Apply Stirling to each genuinely large argument
Cancel extensive terms carefully in logarithmic form
Retain square-root and finite-index factors when ratios or peak widths require them
Expand the specified dilute or nearly balanced limit
Check against exact values or state the controlled asymptotic accuracy
methods.boundary: Leading entropy accuracy does not imply small relative error in the multiplicity itself. Do not apply Stirling to a small occupation number merely because total particle number is large.

methods.title: Evaluate canonical energy fluctuations and size scaling
methods.principle: Energy variance equals k T squared times heat capacity
steps: Determine the appropriate heat capacity of the system
Insert it into the canonical variance relation
Compute the standard deviation and divide by mean energy if requested
Evaluate size or temperature scaling
Check whether the reservoir and ensemble assumptions apply
methods.boundary: A macroscopic fractional fluctuation shrinks with system size for an extensive heat capacity; the result does not assert zero microscopic fluctuations.

methods.title: Thermal wavelength versus particle separation
methods.principle: de Broglie wavelength and thermal kinetic energy
steps: Estimate the thermal momentum and de Broglie wavelength.
Obtain particle separation directly or from ideal-gas number density.
Compare wavelength and separation; solve for a threshold temperature and assess the stated system.
methods.boundary: Distinct from deciding freeze-out by comparing a discrete level spacing to kT.

methods.title: Evaluate a supplied ideal two-level thermal response
methods.principle: Population imbalance is set by the level splitting divided by kT
steps: Form the dimensionless half-splitting over kT
Evaluate polarization, energy or heat capacity from the supplied response
Compute entropy from the populations or equivalent hyperbolic expression
Normalize by the requested maximum
Invert the response for a target polarization or temperature
Check saturation and high-temperature limits
methods.boundary: An electron or nuclear moment changes the physical scale, not the evaluation sequence; the actual nuclear number of states must match the explicitly imposed model.

methods.title: Derive energy moments and fluctuations from partition derivatives
methods.principle: Differentiating a Boltzmann weight brings down its energy
steps: Write the canonical partition sum with temperature-independent energies and fixed external parameters
Differentiate with respect to inverse temperature
Divide by Z to identify first and second energy moments
Form derivatives of log Z for the cumulants
Convert inverse-temperature derivatives to temperature response
Derive the heat-capacity fluctuation relation
methods.boundary: Canonical variance is k T squared times heat capacity under the specified fixed constraints; distinguish a derivation from direct use of the resulting formula.

methods.title: Estimate paramagnetic cooling and its internal-field limit
methods.principle: Independent-spin entropy depends on magnetic energy divided by temperature
steps: Infer the spin-entropy scale from magnetic moment and field
Hold the entropy parameter fixed during ideal demagnetization
Relate final temperature to the effective final field
Estimate internal dipolar fields from moment and neighbor spacing
Explain low-temperature deviations and sensitivity to parasitic heat
methods.boundary: The internal-field estimate is order of magnitude and depends on geometry and interactions; the entropy-slope maximum is not identical to the heat-capacity maximum.

methods.title: Relate ideal-gas states in quasistatic adiabatic compression or expansion
methods.principle: First law with Q=0 and constant active degree count
steps: Check that the gas change is quasistatic and adiabatic with constant active heat capacities
Determine gamma from the active degrees of freedom
Use the established PV^gamma or TV^(gamma-1) relation with the ideal-gas equation to connect the given endpoints
Set heat to zero and obtain signed work from the internal-energy change
Compare endpoints and work with a specified alternative path when requested
methods.boundary: PV to the gamma is not valid for arbitrary irreversible adiabatic changes or changing heat capacities.

methods.title: Derive a gas sound speed from the appropriate bulk modulus
methods.principle: B=-V dP/dV and sound speed squared=B/rho
steps: Differentiate the equation of state along the stated thermal constraint
Compare isothermal and adiabatic bulk moduli
Choose the constraint relevant to a fast sound disturbance
Substitute ideal-gas density
Compare thermal molecular and sound speeds and state remaining parameter dependence

methods.title: Balance sensible and latent heat across temperature and phase changes
methods.principle: The sum of signed material energy changes equals the specified external input
steps: Choose all bodies and state the constant-pressure or constant-volume constraint
Identify initial phases and temperatures and propose the final phase branch
Express each signed sensible change using its appropriate heat capacity and add every latent transformation stage
Sum the changes and equate them to the specified heat or converted external input,which is zero for an isolated mixture
Solve the unknown temperature,phase fraction,heat capacity,mass or supplied energy
Check the final phase,temperature interval and signs;repeat on another branch if the assumed phase is impossible
methods.boundary: Constant-pressure latent heat is an enthalpy change. Use the heat capacity appropriate to the actual constraint;independent mechanical work and path-dependent gas work remain cross-listed. A final mixed phase stays at the transition temperature until its latent budget is exhausted.

methods.title: Find chemical potential from an entropy or energy function
methods.principle: mu=-T partial S/partial N at U,V, or partial U/partial N at S,V
steps: Identify particle number and the held-fixed energy and geometry
Retain all explicit and implicit number dependence in the state function
Differentiate before replacing energy by its temperature expression
Simplify into temperature and density
Interpret changes with concentration or an added external potential
Check per-particle versus molar convention
methods.boundary: For a gravitational system the fixed total energy contains N mgz; differentiating thermal energy as if total energy were independent of N misses the potential term.

methods.title: Derive or apply the slope of a coexistence boundary
methods.principle: Equal phase potentials remain equal along coexistence
steps: Set the relevant molar potentials equal
Differentiate their equality along the phase boundary
Solve the slope from entropy and conjugate-variable differences
Replace entropy difference by latent heat over temperature when appropriate
Integrate or linearize over the stated range
Interpret signs and zero-temperature or critical limits
methods.boundary: The magnetic analogue has a different conjugate sign from pressure-volume work. Constant slopes give local estimates unless a constant-difference model is explicitly imposed.

methods.title: Derive a dilute freezing shift from solvent chemical potentials
methods.principle: Solute lowers the solvent chemical potential
steps: Write equality of solid and liquid solvent chemical potentials at coexistence
Lower the liquid solvent chemical potential by its dilute ideal-mixing contribution,while the solid remains pure solvent
Expand both pure-phase chemical potentials about the pure-solvent freezing point
Use their temperature derivatives as negative entropies and relate the entropy difference to latent heat
Solve the linearized coexistence equation for the negative freezing-temperature shift and explain its sign
methods.boundary: The solid is pure solvent and excludes solute;the solution is dilute. Applying this established law numerically is listed separately from deriving it. The Raoult-plus-Clapeyron boiling proof is also separate.

methods.title: Derive boiling elevation from vapor-pressure lowering
methods.principle: Raoult pressure lowering and the Clausius-Clapeyron saturation slope
steps: Use the dilute nonvolatile-solute fraction to obtain the decrease in solvent vapor pressure at the pure boiling temperature
Identify boiling as equality of solvent vapor pressure with the fixed external pressure
Linearize the vapor-pressure increase produced by a small temperature rise
Insert the Clausius-Clapeyron slope with the stated ideal-vapor and latent-heat approximations
Equate the pressure recovery to the Raoult decrease and solve for the positive temperature shift
methods.boundary: This is the explicitly requested pressure-slope proof. It is distinct from expanding equal solid and liquid chemical potentials for freezing.

methods.title: Construct phase coexistence from free-energy curves
methods.principle: The stable extensive mixture is the lower convex envelope
steps: Write free energy of separated phases as a weighted straight-line combination
Enforce equality of tangent slope and intercept at phase endpoints
Identify coexistence endpoints and the lower envelope
Repeat across temperature to build phase boundaries
Identify critical, azeotropic, eutectic or peritectic topology from which tangencies meet
Distinguish phase composition from total composition
methods.boundary: A free-energy crossing alone does not determine binary coexistence compositions. Retain the actual source topology rather than substituting a generic two-phase lens.

methods.title: Calculate steady conductive heat flow through one or more regions
methods.principle: Fourier law and equal steady flow through layers in series
steps: Identify the temperature difference and conductivity geometry
Integrate or use the uniform-layer thermal resistance
Add series resistances and parallel heat-flow paths correctly
Recover interface temperature differences or total power
Convert energy over time into a requested cost
Check whether convection invalidates a still-medium model
methods.boundary: The building R value is resistance per unit area, not the total K/W resistance; a bulk empty air gap can convect.

methods.title: Explain physical limits of low-temperature cooling
methods.principle: Entropy removal, heat leaks and vanishing available cooling channels
steps: Identify the working cooling mechanism
Track how its entropy or heat-removal capacity changes at low temperature
Include the limiting field, vapor pressure or temperature-dependent transport scale
Compare with unavoidable heat inputs
Separate a model breakdown from a general unattainability claim
methods.boundary: Vanishing heat capacity alone is not a complete proof that absolute zero is unattainable; the cooling dynamics and finite resources matter.

methods.title: Extract critical scaling from a local equation-of-state expansion
methods.principle: Leading nonzero Taylor terms govern the mean-field singularity
steps: Expand in reduced temperature and order-parameter displacement
Retain terms according to consistent near-critical scaling
Solve coexistence or symmetry conditions
Obtain order-parameter and latent-heat scaling
Evaluate critical-isotherm and response-function powers
Specify the thermodynamic path used for response exponents
methods.boundary: For van der Waals compressibility use the critical isochore above Tc and a homogeneous coexistence branch below Tc, not the flat two-phase mixture segment.

methods.title: Derive the performance of a specified thermodynamic path cycle
methods.principle: Net work and positive external heat input follow from every path segment
steps: Identify endpoint states, cycle direction and each leg constraint
Use equations of state and adiabatic relations to link endpoints
Compute heat and work on every leg
Check for a heat-flow sign change INSIDE a leg and split its heat integrals when needed
Sum positive external heat separately from heat rejected
Divide useful output by the appropriate input: net work over heat input for an engine, or specified cooling load over work input for a refrigerator
Compare with a reservoir bound without replacing the requested path derivation
methods.boundary: Regenerative internal exchange is excluded from external heat only if a regenerator is specified. A positive net heat for a leg does not prove that heat entered throughout that leg. A refrigerator contacting a continuum of temperatures needs an explicit definition of its useful cooling load. Different required path derivations remain explicit subtasks.

methods.title: Account for energy flow and performance of cyclic devices
methods.principle: A complete cycle has zero internal-energy change
steps: Choose the device and surroundings boundary
Assign signed heat and work transfers
Use a supplied or established performance law when given,including the ideal Otto relation between efficiency,gamma and compression ratio;invert it for the requested device parameter
Enforce zero net cycle energy change
Form useful output divided by paid input
Convert heat loads to mass-flow or temperature changes when requested
methods.boundary: Efficiency, refrigerator COP and heat-pump COP have different numerators. An open refrigerator within a closed room adds its electrical input as net room heat.

methods.title: Prove a second-law bound by combining cyclic devices
methods.principle: Scale and cancel a shared heat or work transfer
steps: Orient the proposed device and a reversible reference cycle
Scale their cycle rates to cancel the selected shared transfer
Sum all remaining reservoir heats and work
Identify the forbidden isolated effect
State which second-law formulation is contradicted
methods.boundary: Cancel the appropriate transfer explicitly; a verbal claim that one device is better than Carnot is not the requested construction.

methods.title: Find an equilibrium concentration profile from equal chemical potentials
methods.principle: Thermal and diffusive equilibrium in an external potential
steps: Write each species chemical potential including its external potential
Set temperatures and chemical potentials equal between positions
Solve the logarithmic density relation
Apply the boundary concentration
Compare with hydrostatic or Boltzmann profiles and state ideal-gas assumptions
methods.boundary: This chemical-potential derivation is distinct from a requested mechanical slab-force derivation, even when both give the same barometric law.

methods.title: Derive escape and depletion through a small aperture
methods.principle: Molecular impact rate with no incoming gas
steps: Relate wall pressure to collision rate and normal momentum transfer
Estimate the incident normal speed using thermal motion
Replace collisions on the removed patch by escaping particles
Insert number density to derive the depletion equation
Integrate at fixed temperature and identify the escape time
State small-aperture and external-pressure assumptions
methods.boundary: The rough rms-component estimate in Schroeder 1.22 is not the exact Maxwell-distribution effusion prefactor. A tire at ambient pressure is only an order-of-magnitude application of the vacuum model.

methods.title: Separate internal-energy change from constant-pressure heat or other work
methods.principle: H=U+PV and delta H=Q+W_other at fixed pressure
steps: Identify the initial and final states and pressure
Obtain the enthalpy change
Calculate the change in PV, using gas-mole changes when applicable
Recover delta U=delta H-delta PV
Track work by the atmosphere and any non-PV work
Keep physical phases explicit

methods.title: Derive an elastic force from configurational entropy
methods.principle: Generalized force is minus T times the entropy derivative at fixed energy
steps: Count constrained polymer configurations
Express orientation count in terms of extension
Write the generalized first-law work sign
Differentiate the entropy with respect to length
Expand the small-extension limit
Analyze constant-load temperature changes and adiabatic stretching with the remaining thermal entropy
methods.boundary: A two-direction chain has no energetic spring in this idealization; extension removes configurational entropy and is not modeled by an arbitrary temperature-independent Hooke constant.

methods.title: Calculate entropy change from heat capacity, latent heat and reservoirs
methods.principle: Integrate reversible dQ/T between the actual endpoint states
steps: Find endpoint temperatures and phases, using an energy balance if necessary
Construct a reversible reference path for each component
Integrate the applicable heat capacity divided by absolute temperature
Add latent energy divided by transition temperature
Add signed reservoir heat over reservoir temperature
Sum all components and distinguish system change from entropy production
methods.boundary: The reference-path heat need not equal the heat in the actual irreversible process. An absolute entropy needs a reference entropy or justified zero-temperature limit.

methods.title: Determine exchange direction and stable equilibrium from entropy
methods.principle: Maximize total entropy under conserved extensive quantities
steps: Express one subsystem variable as total minus the other
Compare the first entropy derivatives to determine the favored transfer direction
Set the total first derivative to zero for equilibrium
Check negative total second derivative for local stability
Translate into equal temperature, pressure or chemical potential only under the appropriate shared constraints
methods.boundary: A stationary point alone is not stable equilibrium. Negative heat capacity is compatible with a sufficiently small positive-heat-capacity partner, not with an arbitrary infinite bath.

methods.title: Compare entropy changes with heat along distinct paths
methods.principle: Entropy is a state function; heat depends on the path
steps: Determine common endpoint states
Compute the system entropy change from a valid state formula
Independently find actual heat and work for each path
Compare delta S with Q/T only under the required isothermal reversible condition
Include environmental changes when interpreting irreversibility
methods.boundary: Free expansion can increase system entropy with Q=0; its entropy change can be evaluated along a different reversible path, but that path heat is not the actual heat.

methods.title: Find the critical point of an equation of state
methods.principle: A critical isotherm has a stationary inflection
steps: Differentiate pressure with respect to volume at fixed temperature
Solve simultaneous first- and second-derivative conditions
Substitute into the equation of state
Form reduced variables or dimensionless compression factor
Check dimensional conventions for per-molecule versus per-mole constants
methods.boundary: The resulting critical parameters belong to the assumed equation of state and need not quantitatively match the real fluid.

methods.title: Evaluate and compare a supplied nonideal equation of state
methods.principle: An explicit equation relates pressure, temperature, density and material parameters
steps: Identify whether constants refer to particles or moles
Insert the actual state in the complete given equation of state
Check excluded-volume and physical-phase domain conditions
Evaluate the requested pressure, temperature or volume
Compare with the corresponding ideal-gas value and state the percentage denominator
Explain attractive and excluded-volume contributions
methods.boundary: Using the full equation is not the same task as deriving a virial expansion or locating critical/coexistence parameters. A value on a homogeneous van der Waals branch does not certify global phase stability.

methods.title: Explain temperature, thermal contact and heat-transfer mechanisms
methods.principle: Temperature differences drive spontaneous energy exchange, not necessarily equal transient sensations
steps: Identify the interacting bodies, their temperatures and the measured property
Distinguish conduction, bulk-fluid convection and radiation across the actual boundaries
Compare the material conductivity, thermal capacity and relevant geometry
State the common-temperature condition for equilibrium or explain the nonequilibrium exchange
Explain why a transient sensation need not measure temperature
methods.boundary: A cooling-time calculation requires an actual transport and heat-capacity model. Density-driven convection must include the direction of the density contrast; radiation can transfer energy through vacuum. Qualitative comparisons do not certify safe contact or exposure.

methods.title: Use active quadratic degrees of freedom to infer energy, speed or heat capacity
methods.principle: One half kT per active quadratic term
steps: Identify translational, rotational and vibrational quadratic terms
Exclude explicitly frozen modes and count kinetic and potential terms separately
Sum their mean energies for the specified particle count
Obtain rms motion or differentiate energy with respect to temperature as requested
Compare with measured heat capacity and explain model limitations
methods.boundary: A classical degree count is not a quantum freeze-out calculation. Liquids need not have purely quadratic potential energy.

methods.title: Relate temperature change to linear or volume expansion
methods.principle: Fractional expansion coefficients at a specified pressure
steps: Choose the initial length or volume and applicable coefficient
Compute the small temperature-induced change
Match constrained geometrical changes or compare expansion of joined materials
Retain coefficient sign and temperature dependence
For a volume-coefficient derivation differentiate the product of the three dimensions
methods.boundary: A density anomaly also needs buoyancy and mixing reasoning; the number of expansion directions is not a new type.

methods.title: Use homogeneous scaling and the Euler relation
methods.principle: Extensive variables scale together while intensive variables stay fixed
steps: Specify which extensive variables scale and which intensive variables remain fixed
Apply a common scale factor to the function
Classify the scaling of the result
Differentiate the scaling identity to obtain an Euler relation when required
Check number-density or composition dependence
methods.boundary: Doubling particle number at fixed volume is not the extensivity operation. Surface and long-range interaction terms require care.

methods.title: Optimize a finite-rate endoreversible engine
methods.principle: Reversible working fluid with irreversible finite-temperature heat transfer
steps: Write heat-transfer laws with the specified contact times
Relate working-fluid heats by its reversible entropy balance
Express useful power per full cycle time
Eliminate one working-fluid temperature
Differentiate power within the allowed temperature interval
Evaluate efficiency at the maximum and compare with the reversible zero-power bound
methods.boundary: The square-root temperature efficiency follows from the specified equal-contact-time linear-transfer model, not from a universal efficiency-at-maximum-power law.

methods.title: Distinguish heat, work and stored energy
methods.principle: Energy conservation with a specified system boundary
steps: Choose the system and energy-transfer boundary
Identify spontaneous temperature-driven transfer versus other work
Write the signed first-law balance;for an open boundary include the energy carried by entering and leaving matter as well as heat and work
Determine what the given endpoint information does or does not fix
Supply an example or explain the missing path information
methods.boundary: A temperature rise does not prove that heat entered; microwave and electrical energy transfer are work under this textbook convention. A vented vessel does not retain a fixed particle count;flowing matter can carry enthalpy even without heat crossing the wall.

methods.title: Calculate a steady-flow thermal cycle using enthalpies
methods.principle: Flow work is included in enthalpy
steps: Label every inlet and outlet state
Apply the appropriate isentropic, isobaric or isenthalpic component constraint
Obtain enthalpies and entropies from tables
Compute each heater heat and turbine or compressor work per unit mass
Include pump or expander work under the stated approximation
Form efficiency or COP and scale by mass-flow rate
methods.boundary: A real adiabatic turbine increases entropy; adiabatic is not synonymous with isentropic. Keep net work distinct from gross turbine output.

methods.title: Find saturation, dew point or condensation during mixing and ascent
methods.principle: Actual vapor partial pressure is compared with saturation vapor pressure
steps: Determine actual vapor pressure from initial humidity
Obtain saturation pressure versus temperature
Track actual vapor pressure under the specified mixing or parcel-expansion constraints
Find a crossing or tangency with the saturation curve
Interpret condensation onset and any environmental-humidity bound
methods.boundary: A rising closed parcel has changing total and vapor partial pressure before condensation. Holding the initial vapor pressure fixed during ascent is only an extra approximation.

methods.title: Infer state, amount or density of a dilute gas
methods.principle: PV=NkT=nRT
steps: Choose a consistent absolute pressure and temperature
Identify conserved amount or common pressure between connected regions
Convert mass, moles and particle number as needed
Solve for the requested state variable or density
For separation estimates take the cube root of volume per particle
methods.boundary: The equation of state does not by itself specify heat, work or a process path.

methods.title: Evaluate classical ideal-gas entropy and its validity
methods.principle: Sackur-Tetrode or its dimension-specific phase-space counterpart
steps: Specify particle number, mass, energy and available volume
Convert pressure and temperature inputs through the equation of state and caloric relation
Substitute consistently into the logarithm with dimensionless argument
Take endpoint differences or solve the requested entropy threshold
Check the dilute classical regime and indistinguishability correction
methods.boundary: A negative classical entropy at low temperature signals failure of the classical formula, not a physical negative microstate count.

methods.title: Derive constrained thermodynamic derivatives from the fundamental differential
methods.principle: Match coefficients in dU=T dS-P dV+mu dN and transformed potentials
steps: Write the appropriate thermodynamic differential and identify independent variables
Hold the specified variables fixed
Match the remaining coefficient or use a chain rule
Form dH when pressure rather than volume is fixed
Relate entropy derivatives to heat capacities or forces
Preserve generalized work signs
methods.boundary: A differential identity relates neighboring equilibrium states; it does not automatically equate actual irreversible heat to T dS.

methods.title: Explain where entropy is produced in a specified process
methods.principle: Include all affected bodies and irreversible transfer mechanisms
steps: Identify the physical changes rather than visual disorder alone
Locate mixing, friction, chemical conversion or heat flow through finite temperature differences
Include surroundings and energy dissipation
Explain why simply reversing the visible motion does not restore the full state
Separate qualitative sign reasoning from a quantitative entropy calculation
methods.boundary: A visibly tidier or broken object alone does not establish the universe entropy change without its interactions.

methods.title: Determine adiabatic parcel cooling and convective stability
methods.principle: Adiabatic parcel relation combined with hydrostatic pressure balance
steps: Derive dT/dP for a moving parcel
Match its pressure to the surrounding atmosphere
Use hydrostatic dP/dz
Obtain the dry adiabatic temperature gradient
Compare the environmental gradient with the parcel gradient for stability
methods.boundary: The parcel cools adiabatically, even when the background atmosphere is not isentropic.

methods.title: Determine phase fractions by component conservation
methods.principle: Total composition is the weighted average of phase compositions
steps: Write total amount and component amount balances
Substitute the endpoint phase compositions
Solve the two phase amounts or their ratio
Interpret the complementary tie-line distances
Check endpoints and the composition unit convention
methods.boundary: A liquid-to-gas ratio is not the same as the liquid fraction of the total.

methods.title: Find liquid-gas coexistence from an isotherm and equal Gibbs energy
methods.principle: Equal-area construction enforces equal chemical potentials
steps: Find the competing volumes on a subcritical isotherm
Solve equal pressure and zero integrated excess pressure between them
Identify the coexistence pressure
Independently construct G(P) from the equation of state
Check the equal-G crossing
Replace the unstable homogeneous segment by phase coexistence
methods.boundary: The van der Waals loop contains locally unstable and metastable branches; do not call every homogeneous branch locally unstable merely because it is above the global minimum.

methods.title: Derive or use a Maxwell relation
methods.principle: Mixed partial derivatives of a smooth potential commute
steps: Choose a potential with the needed natural variables
Identify its first derivatives from the fundamental differential
Equate mixed derivatives with their correct signs
Apply fixed constraints and any limiting entropy condition
State smoothness and phase-region assumptions
methods.boundary: A relation valid within one smooth phase cannot be applied across a first-order jump without treating the discontinuity.

methods.title: Derive ideal-mixture entropy from species expansion or composition counting
methods.principle: Independent distinct species gain accessible configurations on mixing
steps: Identify distinguishable species and their conserved particle counts
For gas expansion assign each species its initial and final accessible volume
Alternatively count assignments of species to equivalent sites
Sum logarithmic entropy gains and simplify to mole fractions
Check pure and equal-mixture limits
Explain why identical species do not produce the same extensive mixing term
methods.boundary: The expansion and combinatorial derivations are explicitly distinguished in task rows when the source prescribes one. Equal molecular size and equivalent interactions are assumptions for ideal dense mixtures.

methods.title: Find a nucleation barrier and critical droplet size
methods.principle: Bulk free-energy gain competes with surface energy cost
steps: Write the bulk chemical-potential change proportional to droplet volume
Add surface tension times area
Differentiate with respect to radius
Classify the nonzero extremum and growth/shrink directions
Express vapor chemical-potential excess through supersaturation
Estimate the critical size and barrier implications
methods.boundary: The nonzero critical droplet at supersaturation is unstable, not a stable equilibrium droplet; relative humidity equal to one refers to a flat interface.

methods.title: Calculate or infer a dilute-solution osmotic pressure
methods.principle: Equal solvent chemical potentials require an extra solution pressure
steps: Count independently dissolved solute particles including dissociation
Use the solvent chemical-potential depression and pressure derivative
Obtain osmotic pressure from particle concentration
Balance with hydrostatic pressure or invert for molar mass
Integrate reversible separation work with the actual concentration path
Check dilution and compressibility assumptions
methods.boundary: Constant-feed pressure times extracted volume is a reservoir approximation. Complete finite-batch separation changes concentration and eventually exceeds the dilute model.

methods.title: Read phase changes and coexistence on a supplied phase diagram
methods.principle: Equilibrium regions and coexistence boundaries determine the phases along the stated path
steps: Identify diagram axes and the controlled pressure, temperature or composition
Trace the requested path and locate every boundary crossing
For a pure material distinguish melting, vaporization and sublimation and the triple and critical points
For a mixture read the tie-line endpoints for coexisting compositions
Use conservation for phase fractions when needed and distinguish phase removal from closed-system evolution
Explain the corresponding physical state and qualify extrapolation beyond the supplied diagram
methods.boundary: A p-T pure-substance diagram and a mixture composition diagram have different axes; tie-line composition steps apply only to the latter. Bulk liquid below a pure substance triple-point pressure is not an equilibrium phase. Metastability, salts and confinement are separate assumptions.

methods.title: Locate pure-phase stability and crossings from Gibbs energies
methods.principle: The equilibrium phase has the lowest molar Gibbs energy
steps: Use common-reference Gibbs energies at a reference state
Integrate dG=-S dT+V dP under the specified material approximation
Compare candidate phase values and solve equalities
Reject crossings hidden above a lower third phase
Sketch slopes and the stable lower envelope
State extrapolation and metastability limits
methods.boundary: Continuous G can have discontinuous slopes at a first-order transition. Constant-volume and constant-entropy-difference extrapolations are assumptions, not globally exact equations of state.

methods.title: Recover a fluid state from tables and mixture constraints
methods.principle: Specific state functions interpolate by vapor mass fraction
steps: Identify the specified pressure, temperature and phase
Locate or interpolate the correct single-phase table entries
Test whether a conserved state function lies between saturated-liquid and vapor values
Solve the linear quality relation in the two-phase region
Recover the remaining state functions and report interpolation assumptions
methods.boundary: Quality is a mass fraction for mass-specific tables and a mole fraction for molar tables. Do not extend an ideal-gas formula through a liquid-vapor transition.

methods.title: Determine equilibrium tendency from system plus reservoir entropy
methods.principle: Reservoir constraints select the potential that decreases
steps: Write total entropy change including the reservoir
Use conservation of energy, volume and particles as applicable
Substitute the reservoir temperature, pressure and chemical potential
Identify the corresponding potential difference
Compare candidate states or slopes at fixed natural variables
Distinguish thermodynamic preference from kinetics or small-system fluctuations
methods.boundary: An equilibrium preference neither guarantees a rapid transition nor removes finite-system probability fluctuations.

methods.title: Evaluate thermodynamic potentials and available work
methods.principle: Choose the potential appropriate to the environmental constraints
steps: Obtain energy, entropy, pressure and volume for the specified state
Form H=U+PV, F=U-TS or G=H-TS
Take differences with a consistent reference
Relate minus the appropriate free-energy change to maximum extracted work
Use the entropy change to determine reversible heat
Distinguish actual irreversible output from the state-function bound
methods.boundary: G bounds non-expansion work at fixed T,P; F bounds total work at fixed T. A change in device efficiency does not change a state-function difference between the same endpoints.

methods.title: Find the vapor-pressure shift caused by an inert gas
methods.principle: Equal liquid and vapor chemical potentials at different total and partial pressures
steps: Differentiate the coexistence condition at fixed temperature
Express the liquid chemical-potential change through molecular volume times total-pressure change
Express the ideal vapor change through kT times its logarithmic partial-pressure change
Integrate with a reference coexistence state
Evaluate and assess the small-effect approximation
methods.boundary: The inert gas is insoluble and the vapor ideal; this is an isothermal pressure correction, not the temperature-dependent vapor-pressure equation.

methods.title: Compute work, energy and heat along a specified thermodynamic path
methods.principle: W_on=-integral P_ext dV and delta U=Q+W_on
steps: Read the directed path and its constraints
Integrate pressure along each volume-changing leg
Compute endpoint internal-energy differences using the correct material model
Obtain heat from the signed first law
Sum legs for a cycle and check that its total state-function change vanishes
Explain the physical heating or piston operations
methods.boundary: Use gas pressure in the work integral only for a quasistatic path. A diagram or explicit P(V) is required; endpoints alone do not fix work.

methods.title: Separate regenerated heat from external cycle heat
methods.principle: An ideal cyclic heat store returns its absorbed heat
steps: Identify the two complementary internal heating and cooling legs
Match their heat capacities and temperature ranges
Track heat stored and returned over a full cycle
Remove only that matched heat from external input and rejection
Recompute efficiency and discuss finite-transfer practical limits
methods.boundary: Perfect regeneration is an idealization; a regenerator does not itself supply net energy per cycle.

methods.title: Derive a regular-solution free energy and miscibility gap
methods.principle: Mean-field pair energies compete with ideal mixing entropy
steps: Count each neighboring pair once
Weight like and unlike pair probabilities by composition
Subtract the unmixed energy
Add ideal mixing entropy to form free energy
Locate loss of convexity and the critical mixing temperature
Determine coexistence compositions by common tangents and plot the phase boundary
methods.boundary: The spinodal inflection curve is not the binodal coexistence curve. A symmetric model allows a horizontal common tangent but not arbitrary use of its inflection points as phase compositions.

methods.title: Bound cyclic engine or refrigerator performance using reservoir entropy
methods.principle: Total reservoir entropy cannot decrease
steps: Write the cycle energy balance
Express each reservoir entropy change as signed heat divided by its absolute temperature
Impose nonnegative total entropy production
Eliminate unwanted heats to bound the requested performance
Identify equality with reversible operation
methods.boundary: A cycle contacting a range of temperatures cannot automatically be treated as contacting only two fixed reservoirs. Finite-source cooling and heating require integration for an attainable reversible result.

methods.title: Relate heat capacities and compressibilities by constrained derivatives
methods.principle: Chain rules and Maxwell relations eliminate inaccessible derivatives
steps: Choose the explicitly requested entropy or energy differential route
Expand in a convenient independent-variable pair
Impose the requested constant-pressure, volume or entropy constraint
Eliminate cross derivatives using Maxwell and cyclic identities
Express the result through measurable expansion and compressibility coefficients
Check ideal-gas and stable-material limits
methods.boundary: Keep the entropy-based and energy/enthalpy-based derivations distinguishable when a problem explicitly requests one. Positivity arguments require a mechanically stable phase.

methods.title: Determine stream fractions from whole-device energy conservation
methods.principle: Enthalpy flux is conserved in an insulated steady-flow assembly
steps: Choose a control volume enclosing the stated heat exchanger and valves
List inlet and outlet stream rates and enthalpies
Enforce mass conservation
Enforce energy conservation with any external work or heat
Solve the desired liquid fraction or flow ratio
Check physical bounds
methods.boundary: A regenerative liquefier is not equivalent to a single throttle at the initial feed temperature.

methods.title: Find energy and entropy changes in rapid irreversible compression
methods.principle: Actual external work and state-function entropy after re-equilibration
steps: Compute work from the specified applied force and boundary displacement
Decide whether the short event is thermally isolated
Apply the first law with the stated energy destination
Obtain the equilibrium volume and energy increments
Use the thermodynamic identity for a small change or an exact endpoint entropy formula
Compare actual work with quasistatic pressure work
methods.boundary: Do not insert an adiabatic reversible PV-gamma relation for a sudden dissipative process. State whether quoted force includes the full external load.

methods.title: Calibrate and compare temperature scales
methods.principle: Affine calibration and the special meaning of absolute zero
steps: Identify the two calibration points or degree size and zero
Solve for the linear scale factor and offset
Convert the specified temperatures
Distinguish an absolute temperature ratio from a temperature difference
methods.boundary: A ratio such as twice the temperature is not invariant under an arbitrary shift of zero.

methods.title: Find temperature and phase after throttling
methods.principle: Steady insulated throttling conserves enthalpy when kinetic and potential changes are negligible
steps: Compute inlet enthalpy at its pressure and temperature
Set outlet enthalpy equal to inlet enthalpy
Locate the outlet-pressure single-phase or saturation branch
Interpolate temperature or solve phase quality
Assess cooling versus heating and the available table range
methods.boundary: Throttling is not an isentropic expansion and need not cool the fluid.

methods.title: Integrate or use a vapor-pressure law
methods.principle: Clapeyron with ideal vapor and negligible condensed volume
steps: Apply the ideal-gas volume to the coexistence relation
State the constant latent-heat approximation
Integrate log pressure versus inverse temperature
Determine the reference constant from coexistence data
Invert for boiling temperature or combine with an ambient pressure profile
Compare with table values to assess the approximation
methods.boundary: Do not extrapolate this model through a critical point, a different condensed phase, or a broad range with strongly varying latent heat.

methods.title: Compare an equation of state with a low-density virial expansion
methods.principle: Expansion in inverse molar volume
steps: Identify the dilute expansion parameter
Expand the proposed equation of state consistently
Match coefficients of inverse molar-volume powers
Evaluate the first correction and its validity
Relate correction signs to attractive and excluded-volume effects
methods.boundary: A numerical coefficient fit is retained separately when the problem requires fitting data.

methods.title: Derive moist-adiabatic cooling with latent heat feedback
methods.principle: First-law parcel expansion coupled to saturation and hydrostatic pressure
steps: Include latent heat released by decreasing vapor content in the parcel energy balance
Express saturated vapor fraction in terms of vapor pressure and total pressure
Differentiate along the rising parcel
Use Clausius-Clapeyron for the vapor-pressure derivative
Eliminate the pressure gradient using hydrostatic balance
Evaluate and interpret dry-limit and warm/cold differences
methods.boundary: This derivation retains the stated dilute-vapor and ideal-air assumptions; it is not the dry lapse-rate derivation with an arbitrary smaller heat capacity.

methods.title: Explain correlated electrical and thermal conduction through mobile carriers
methods.principle: Mobile particles can transport both charge and energy
steps: Identify the carriers available in each material
Determine whether those carriers can transport net charge and thermal energy
Relate their mobility and scattering qualitatively to the observed conduction
Retain neutral or lattice carriers of heat when explaining exceptions
methods.boundary: Good thermal conduction does not imply electrical conduction; lattice vibrations can carry heat without net charge. Deriving a transport coefficient is a separate task.

methods.title: Verify and interpret a supplied diffusion profile
methods.principle: Direct PDE substitution and conservation of integrated excess
steps: Differentiate the supplied profile in time and space
Check the diffusion equation
Identify width and amplitude time dependence
Integrate the excess above background to test conserved content
Sketch profiles at several times and interpret spreading
methods.boundary: Verification of a supplied Gaussian does not require solving an arbitrary initial-boundary-value problem.

methods.title: Derive a diffusion equation from local conservation
methods.principle: Storage change equals incoming minus outgoing gradient-driven flux
steps: Choose a thin control volume
Write fluxes through both faces
Equate their difference to accumulation
Take the spatial limit
Substitute Fourier or Fick gradient law
Identify the diffusivity and state assumptions on side losses and coefficients
methods.boundary: Heat and particle diffusion share the same steps after replacing storage density and flux units.

methods.title: Estimate spreading distance or time
methods.principle: Diffusive distance squared is of order diffusivity times time
steps: Identify the transported quantity and its diffusivity
Obtain thermal diffusivity from conductivity divided by volumetric heat capacity if needed
Relate the characteristic length and time
Evaluate the scale with consistent units
Compare with convective or bulk transport and state order-one uncertainty
methods.boundary: An order-of-magnitude spreading time is not a unique boundary-value solution or exact burn threshold.

methods.title: Infer molecular size and number from macroscopic transport data
